BBMB. Moreover, as per respondents Beas Control Board was constituted in the year 960. BCB was constituted in 
the year !966 and all the projects were transferred from Beas Control Board to BCB in the year 966 thereafter as per 
Section 79 of the Punjab Re-organization Act, BMB was constituted for administrative, maintenance and operation of 
various works as mentioned in Section 79 itself. Section 80(6) of the Punjab Re-organization Act provides that BMB 
constituted under Section 79 of the Act shall be re-named as BBMB when any of the components of the Beas Project 
has been transferred under sub-section 5 and the BCB shall cease to exist when all the component of the Beas Project 
have been so transferred. All the projects under BCB were completed in the year 984 and BCB ceased to exist in 
984. When all work of BCB stands transferred to BBMB so it cannot be said that BBMB is separate identity than 
BCB. Rather BCB has merged in BBMB. Moreover, Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaswant Singh case (supra) in 
respect of work charged employees has no where stated that relief can be sought by work charged employees only 
against the BCB. So contention of Ld. AR of the management that BCB and BBMB are two separate entities is 
devoid of merit. 


27. So far this argument of Law Officer for the respondents that the case is hopelessly time barred is concerned, 
the same is again devoid of merits as there was non-compliance of Rule 77 and 78 of Industrial Rules which has been 
reproduced above. Moreover, there is no limitation period prescribed for filing a reference. Moreover, reference was 
received in the year 209. So far as case laws on the point of limitation the same are not attracted in the present case 
as there was no compliance of Judgment of Jaswant Singh case (Supra). Moreover, limitation was added in Section 
2A of the Act in the year 20!0 (5.09.200) and deceased workman was dismissed from service on 25.0.978 and 
AR for respondents has failed to bring this fact that the aforesaid provision was retrospective. 


28. It is added here that in the present case, the reference was made under clause (d) of sub-section (I) of Section 
0 of the Act. It is not case filed under Section 2-A of the Act. Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as 


Raghubir Singh V/s General Manager, Haryana Roadways, Hissar (supra) has held as follow: 


“42. It is an undisputed fact that the dispute was raised by the workman after he was acquitted in the criminal case 
which was initiated at the instance of the respondent. Raising the industrial dispute belatedly and getting the same 
referred from the State Government to the Labour Court is for justifiable reason and the same is supported by law 
laid down by this Court in Calcutta Dock Labour Board (supra). Even assuming for the sake of the argument that 
there was a certain delay and latches on the part of the workman in raising the industrial dispute and getting the 
same referenced for adjudication, the Labour Court is statutorily duty bound to answer the points of dispute referred 
to it by adjudicating the same on merits of the case and it ought to have moulded the relief appropriately in favour of 
the workman. That has not been done at all by the Labour Court. Both the learned single Judge as well as the 
Division Bench of the High Court in its Civil Writ Petition and the Letters Patent Appeal have failed to consider this 
important aspect of the matter.” 


Even Hon'ble Supreme Court in para no.3! of the said judgment has held as follow: 


ढ#उ7, The rejection of the reference by the Labour Court by answering the additional issue no. 2 regarding the 
delay latches and limitation without adjudicating the points of dispute referred to it on the merits amounts to 
failure to exercise its statutory power under Section IIA of the Act. Therefore, we have to interfere with the 
impugned award of the Labour Court and the judgment & order of the High Court as it has erroneously 
confirmed the award of the Labour Court without examining the relevant provisions of the Act and decisions of 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 5053 
this Court referred to supra on the relevant issue regarding the limitation.” 

29. Hon'ble Supreme Court has also referred in the said case decision of Ajaib Singh v. The Sirhind Co- 

Operative Marketing Cum- Processing Service Society Limited & Anr.(AIR ॥/999 Supreme Court ॥357), wherein, 

Court has opined that relief cannot be denied to the workman merely on the ground of delay, stating that:- 
#॥09, It follows, therefore, that the provisions of Article ॥37 of the Schedule to Limitation Act, /963 are not 
applicable to the proceedings under the act and that the relief under it cannot be denied to the workman merely 
on the ground of delay. The plea of delay if raised by the employer is required to be proved as a matter of fact 
by showing the real prejudice and not as a merely hypothetical defence. No reference to the labour court can be 
generally questioned on the ground of delay alone. Even in a case where the delay in shown to be existing, the 
tribunal, labour court or board, dealing with the case can appropriately mould the relief by declining to grant 
back wages to the workman till the date he raised the demand regarding his illegal retrenchment/ termination 
or dismissal. 


30. In view of the aforesaid observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the delay was not thus fatal to the case 
of the appellant. It is also added here that so far as the case Ram Chand Vs. The BBMB and another (supra), 
Ghunghriya Ram versus Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Limited_and_others (supra) and Mr._D 
Poomaran versus The General Manager, Bharat Petorloum Corporation Ltd. and others (supra) referred by the 


AR for respondents are concerned, those cases were filed by the workman under Section 2-A of the Act, which 
specifically provides limitation of 3 years from the date of dismissal or retrenchment. Section l0(l) of the Act 
specifically provide that appropriate government may refer any industrial dispute at any time, whereas the same is 
conspicuously absent in sub-section (3) of Section 2A, which could clearly depict the intention of the legislature 
namely, it had deliberately imposed limitation period under sub-section (3) of Section 2A. Thus, period of limitation 
cannot be considered. So far as the case law titled as Chief Engineer Ranjit Sagar Dam _& Anr. Vs. Sham Lal 
(supra), the same is not attracted to the facts and circumstance of the present case in view of the judgment Raghubir 
Singh V/s General Manager, Haryana Roadways, Hissar (supra), whose relevant paras are reproduced above. 
Therefore, it cannot be said that case of applicant was beyond limitation. 

3]. However, it is added that Smt. Maya Devi, LR of deceased workman in her affidavit nowhere stated that 
retrenchment compensation was not paid to her husband. In her cross examination, she has stated that she does not 
know when her husband was retrenched and he was paid compensation etc. Remaining silent in her affidavit that her 
husband was not paid any retrenchment compensation meaning thereby that her husband was paid retrenchment 
compensation by the management. Moreover, in written statement, stand of the respondents is that the deceased 
workman was paid all terminal benefits i.e. retrenchment compensation, gratuity and ex-gratia etc. on account of 
retrenchment from BCB as per provisions of the Act and other relevant laws. Thus, it shall be presumed that deceased 
workman was given retrenchment compensation. Even a perusal of service record (MWI/B) of deceased workman 
reveals that he was paid gratuity etc. So, there is no breach of Section 25 F of the Act. 

32. Further, there was non-compliance of Jaswant Singh Case (Supra), Reference No.2C of 97l and Rule 77 
& 78 of Industrial Rules and in this case it would be highly difficult to re-employe the workman. The only remedy left 
is to compensate the workman in term of money. 

33. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case and other connected case of similar nature the 
following scheme of compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 

i. Workcharged employee who has completed 5 years of service or more shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/- along 
with interest @9% per annum as compensation from the date of moving of application till the 
realization of amount. 

il. Workcharged employee who has completed less than 5 years but more than | year would be entitled 
Rs.25,000/- along with interest @9% per annum from the date of moving of application till the 
realization of amount. 

ili. Those employees who have not completed | year will not be entitled for any compensation in the 
present case. 

34. Deceased workman Prabha was employed on 29.04.965 and was retrenched on 25.0.!978 as mentioned in 
Discharge Certificate (Ex.W-l) issued by Sub Divisional Officer, BBMB Sundernagar, and has worked for 3 year 
and about 6 months (more than 5 years), so the applicants are entitled for Rs.50,000/- along with interest @9% per 
annum from the date of moving the application till its realization. 


35. The reference is answered accordingly and stands disposed off. 
36. Let copy of this award be sent to the Appropriate Government as required under Section !7 of the Act for 
publication.

ORDER 


This order is being passed on an application of applicant-workman filed under section 2-A(2) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act (herein-after referred as an Act). 


2: The case of the applicant-workman as per his statement of claim is as follows:- 


That he was working under the |* Party-Management since 28.06.!990 and he was illegally relieved from 
service on 3.03.2009 by the [7 Party-Management, whereas he had been assured by the |“ Party-Management for 
disbursement of his arrear dues as well as his rehabilitation. The |** Party-Management has formulated Service Rules 
and as per the said rule on successful completion of probation on first appointment every employee shall be 
confirmed. As per the rules formulated by the Management the date of retirement from service was 60 years and there 
was no such provision for voluntary retirement scheme, but calling the workman by the Management to submit option 
for VR Scheme was unconstitutional. Though, he did not opt for VR Scheme floated by the Management he was 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 5055 


forced to sign the format for VR Scheme and he was assured for rehabilitation for his livelihood. Since, the action of 
the Management was neither legal nor justified the 27 party-workman raised a dispute before the R.L.C.(C) 
Bhubaneswar on dated 28.!.203 and when the matter was not resolved he had filed this application under section 2- 
A(2) of the Act with a prayer to pass an order of his reinstatement of his service with full back wages. 


3. The case of the 7 Party- Management as per its written statement is as follows:- 


That the present proceeding filed by the applicant under section 2-A(2) of the I.D. Act is not maintainable 
in the eye of law as the same is grossly barred by limitation. The applicant workman has voluntarily opted for Special 
VR Scheme floated by the Management and the workman has received all the benefits under Special V.R. scheme. 
After that the applicant-workman in an afterthought and with ill intention had raised industrial dispute under section 
2A(2) of the I.D. Act which is grossly barred by limitation. The applicant workman has voluntarily taken retirement 
on 3.03.2009 from his service by way of opting special V.R. Scheme floated by the Management and also received 
all the benefits accrued to him, so the allegation of illegal removal from service on 3].03.2009 by the Management is 
false, frivolous and baseless. In the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 20l0 Section 2(A)(2) & (3) are inserted 
for the benefits of the workman to raise his dispute with the management connected with or arising out of discharge, 
dismissal, retrenchment or termination, directly before Labour Court or Tribunal within a specific period of three 
years of such alleged dispute, but the applicant has filed his application much after three years. 


A prayer has been made to reject the application of the applicant-workman on the ground of limitation. 


4. After going through the pleadings of both the parties it is quite apparent that the 27 party-workman/applicant 
has filed this application under section 2-A(2) of the I.D. Act on 28.06.20l6 whereas it is the claim of the applicant 
that he was relieved from service on 3!.03.2009. 


5. At this stage the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss here the provisions of the Section - 2(A)(3) of 
the I.D. Act:- 


Section 2-A(3) of the Act specifically provides that the application referred to in sub-section (2) shall be 
made to the Labour Court or Tribunal before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, 
retrenchment, or otherwise termination of service as specified in sub-section(]). 


6. In the instant case the applicant-workman has raised the dispute under section 2-A(2) of the Act after expiry 
of more than seven years of his alleged termination/retrenchment, so the petition filed by the applicant is not within 
the prescribed period provided under the provisions of the I.D. Act. 


7. After considering all the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal finds and holds that the application 
filed under section 2-A(2) of the I.D. Act is not maintainable as it is time barred. Hence, the application filed under 
section 2-A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is rejected and the case is dismissed. 


8. Order is passed accordingly. 


9. A copy of this order is sent to the appropriate government for notification as required under section |7 of the 
ID. Act, 947. File is consigned to record room.

In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section (l) and Sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the

॥ On receiving Order No. 7,-2202/64/202-॥२((५-॥) dated 4/2/202] from the Government of India 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case No. 30 of 202 was registered on 
4.2.202/0.07.2022 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing 
them to appear and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims. 


2. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, President, Koyala Mazdoor Congress filed written statement on behalf of the dependent 
son of the deceased employee on 08/08/2022. Management of ECL filed their written statement on !7/0/2023. In 
gist, fact of the union’s case is that Dahu Kanu, an employee of ECL bearing UM No. 55030 was posted at Khas 
Kajora Colliery as CCM Driver. He died in harness on 48/05/996. Under clause 9.3.2 of NCWA-VI one dependent 
of the deceased employee is entitled to get employment. Accordingly wife of the deceased employee applied for 
providing employment to her and submitted necessary documents. Management of the company did not provide 
employment to the wife of the deceased employee. Discouraging female dependent from claiming employment, 
management of ECL suggested to the wife of the deceased to apply for employment to the dependent son, Pramod 
Kanu. Wife of Late Dahu Kanu thereafter submitted another application for providing employment to her son, 
Pramod Kanu. Management of ECL processed the employment proposal, held screening test at the colliery level and 
Area level. Pramod Kanu was thereafter referred for his medical examination which was to be held by the Initial 
Medical Examination Board. The IME Board declared the age of Pramod Kanu as seventeen to twenty two years 
which was calculated as nineteen years and six months at the time of Initial Medical Examination. Pramod Kanu also 
submitted several documents including his Birth Registration Certificate, wherein his Date of Birth is recorded as 
0I/07/982 which implies that his age was sixteen years on the date of death of Dahu Kanu. He produced his School 
Leaving Certificate/Transfer Certificate in which his Date of Birth is mentioned as 0/07/982. Janma Kundali 
produced revealed the Date of Birth as 0i/07/982. In the Service Record Excerpt of Dahu Kanu age of his son, Dahu 
Kanu was recorded as two years in the year 987. On request of Pramod Kanu for holding his medical examination 
again, the Apex Medical Board on examining Pramod Kanu assessed his age between twenty to twenty five years as 
on 2/03/2007 i.e. fourteen years and eight months on the date of death of employee. According to the union age of 
the person was sixteen years on the date of death of his father as mentioned above and according to report of the 
Medical Board his age was fourteen years and eight months i.e. near to fifteen years. It is further stated that on the 
date of submitting application for employment, age of Pramod Kanu was above fifteen years and according to the 
provision of clause 9.5.0 of NCWA-VI if age of the dependent son is twelve years on the date of death of employee, 
his name would be maintained in live roster for providing employment and wife of the deceased employee is entitled 
to get Monetary Compensation. It is contended by the union that according to the provision of NCWA Coal India 
Limited is legally bound to provide employment to one dependent of the deceased employee and the claim for 
employment is not based upon compassionate ground. It is disclosed that the union raised Industrial Dispute before 
the ALC (C), Raniganj on 2/07/20i0 which ended in failure and FOC report was sent to the Secretary, Ministry of 
Labour and Employment vide letter No. I/05/20l0-ALCR but unfortunately neither the dispute was referred for 
adjudication nor did the Ministry deny such reference. Concerned union thereafter approached the Ministry afresh for 
referring the Industrial Dispute to the Tribunal. In the Written Statement reference has been made to similar situation

where in a case of Late Sitaram Singh, Hon’ble High Court passed the order and employment was provided to the 
dependent son, though his age was less than fifteen years at the time of death of the employee. Union prayed for 
providing employment to Pramod Kanu as dependent son of Late Dahu Kanu and Monetary Compensation to the wife

3. Management contested the case by filing written statement through Agent, Khas Kajora Colliery, ECL. It is

Compensation to Chandra Kala Devi in lieu of employment under death scheme. In their internal letter dated

2/09/2000 which was returned on 9/05/2003 with a communication that as directed by Headquarters, the colliery 
was requested to process the case of Late Dahu Kanu, Ex-Machine Driver of Khas Kajora Colliery which was claimed 
by the dependent after six months from the date of death of deceased employee for employment after observing all 
formalities. It is further stated that Pramod Kanu claimed employment as son of the deceased employee by submitting 
application on 30/i/2003. A screening of Pramod Kanu was held on 6/02/2004 and relevant papers submitted by 
the son of the deceased were sent to the Area vide letter dated 6/8.03.2004. Initial Medical Examination of Pramod 
Kanu was held on 7/2/2004 where it was found that he was below fifteen years at the time of death of his father and 
the management of Kajora Area informed the Agent by letter dated 04/02/2005 that the claim for employment of 
Pramod Kanu could not be forwarded to Head Quarters. An application was submitted by Pramod Kanu for holding 
his medical examination once again. Initial Medical Examination of Pramod Kanu was done by the Area on 
7/2/2004 and his age was assessed as seventeen to twenty two years and he did not produce his Birth /Birth 
Registration Certificate before the Area Medical Board at that time. He arranged his Birth Registration Certificate 
subsequently which was issued on |8/09/2005 by the authority. On 09/03/2007, Pramod Kanu was referred for his re- 
medical examination by the Apex Medical Board for assessment of his age. On the basis of letter dated 30/05/2007 
issued by the Dy. Chief Personnel Manager of Kajora Area, it was communicated to the Agent, Khas Kajora Colliery 
that earlier Initial Medical Examination of Pramod Kanu was done by the Area Medical Board on [7/2/2004 and his 
age was assessed as seventeen to twenty two years i.e. nineteen years and six months as on [7/2/2004 and on 
referring to the Apex Medical Board for re-examination of his age, Pramod Kanu’s age was assessed by the Apex 
Medical Board as twenty to twenty five years i.e. twenty two years and six months as on [2/03/2007. According to 
the management age of Pramod Kanu was less than fifteen years at the time of death of Late Dahu Kanu and 
according to the rule of the company, son of a deceased employee had to be above fifteen years of age for being 
eligible for entering his name in the live roster for employment. According to the management, Pramod Kanu was 
found ineligible for employment against the death of his deceased father. Furthermore, dispute has been raised more 
than twenty one years after date of death of Late Dahu Kanu and has been referred to this Tribunal in the year 202], 
i.e. after more than twenty three years of death of the employee as such the Industrial Dispute raised is a stale one and 
same needs to be dismissed. Management referred to a decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in a case of M/s. 
Eastern Coalfields Limited vs. Anil Badyakar and Others where the Hon’ble Could disapproved the employment 
on compassionate ground after passage of long years. It was observed that the dispute was a stale and the same was

5. Mr. Proloy Dasgupta is examined as Management Witness-I and filed his affidavit-in-chief. In the affidavit- 
in-chief witness deposed that initially wife of Late Dahu Kanu submitted application for providing employment to her 
but the witness was unable to produce copy of the application. It is deposed that application of the wife of Late Dahu

Management Witness-I produced the following documents in support of their case:- 


(i) copy of application submitted by Pramod Kanu on 28/ [/2003 is produced as Exhibit M-I. 
(ii) copy of service excerpt of Dahu Kanu is produced as Exhibit M-2.

In cross-examination, witness deposed that during pendency of application submitted by the wife of deceased, the son

6. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative argued that Chandra Kala Devi, widow of the deceased employee

Pramod Kanu was less than fifteen years at the time of death of his father (Exhibit W-7). Mr. Kumar submitted that 
Pramod Kanu made a fresh application praying for his re-medical examination by the Apex Medical Board and stated 
that he was sixteen years of age as on |8/05/l998. Manager of Khas Kajora Colliery in letter dated 4/0/2006 
informed Pramod Kanu that Area Medical Board on 7/02/2004 assessed his age as seventeen to twenty two years 


5064 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


and the Birth Registration Certificate which was not produced before the Area Medical Board and was subsequently 
obtained on 8/09/2005 could not be considered. It is further stated in the letter that since age of Pramod Kanu was 
assessed by the Area Medical Board, the same could not be re-examined on the basis of documents not considered to 
be authentic. Mr. Kumar referring to Exhibit W-I, a letter issued by the Manager, Khas Kajora Colliery dated 
08/06/2007 submitted that Pramod Kanu was referred for reassessment of age by the Apex Medical Board and his age 
was assessed as twenty to twenty five years i.e. twenty two years and six months as on |2/03/2007. It is argued that if 
the age assessed by the Medical Board is considered to be correct then average age of Pramod Kanu would be twenty 
two years and six months as on |2/03/2007. Therefore, applying the provision of clause 9.5.0 (iii) of NCWA-VI 
applicable to the workman and the management from 0/07/996 to 30/06/200l, which provides that in a case of 
death if no employment is offered and male dependent is twelve years or more in age, he will be kept in live roster 
and will be provided employment commensurating with his skill and qualification when he attains eighteen years of 
age. Mr. Kumar argued that ECL is bound by NCWA and was responsible to maintain name of the dependent son of 
Late Dahu Kanu in live roster and provide employment to him on his attaining majority. It is argued that in the instant

Monetary Compensation to the widow of the deceased during her lifetime. 


7. Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate for the management of ECL argued that the Industrial Dispute is liable to be 
dismissed on two counts. Firstly, the application for employment was made after inordinate delay of fifteen years and 
secondly the age of the dependent son should not be less than fifteen years for the purpose of maintaining his name in 
live roster. Since the age of Pramod Kanu was thirteen years and eight months at the time of death of his father on 
8/05/998 management had no option but to disapprove the prayer for employment due as petitioner son 
was below age. 


8. I have considered the pleading, evidence adduced and documents produced. Admittedly Dahu Kanu was a 
permanent employment of Khas Kajora Colliery, ECL and died on 8/05/998 while he was in service of the 
company. Chandra Kala Devi, his wife at first submitted application on !0/02/2000 claiming employment. In reply to 
management’s letter No. KKC/P&IR/C-6/46/50 dated 07/02/2000 where after two years from death of employee, 
management asked wife of the deceased that no claim paper for employment had been filed and she filed her 
application only on 25/0/2000 after one and half years as such prayer would not be entertained as per circular and 
guideline of the company, wife of the deceased in letter dated 0/02/2000, explained the delay, disclosing that after 
death of her husband she was in a shock for long time and was not in normal position to take suitable decision. It 
appears from the materials on record that management did not consider the prayer for employment of the wife. 
However, on the basis of application dated 26//2003 by Pramod Kanu (Exhibit W-6) he was referred for his 
medical examination and by letter dated 09/02/2005 (Exhibit W-7), Pramod Kanu was informed by the management 
of Khas Kajora Colliery that on assessment of age by Initial Medical Examination on [7/2/2004 his age was assessed 
between seventeen years to twenty two years i.e. nineteen years six months as on |7/2/2004. It was further informed 
that his prayer could not be forwarded to Head Quarters as he was less than fifteen years of age. Written statement of 
the management reveals that on the basis of application for employment submitted by Pramod Kanu on 30/| ।/2003, 
screening at colliery level was held on !6/02/2004 and his medical examination was held on [7/2/2004. It is evident 
that the application of Pramod Kanu had been entertained and acted upon by the management. He was also referred to 
the Apex Medical Board on 09/03/2007 for his age assessment where his age was reassessed as twenty to twenty five 
years as on |2/03/2007. Management Witness relying upon the age assessed by the Apex Medical Board on 
2/03/2007 (Exhibit M-6) deposed that petitioner was underage at the time of his father’s death and the prayer for 
employment was not allowed. Witness admitted in cross-examination that management did not respond to the 
application of wife praying for employment and Monetary Compensation and no communication was made by the 
management disclosing reasons for not considering the prayers. I find from the evidence that management did not 
communicate their decision to Pramod Kanu regarding his claim for employment. At this juncture it would be 
appropriate to consider the provision of NCWA applicable to a case where death took place on 8/05/998. It appears 
that NCWA-VI which was signed on 23/2/2000 has been made applicable from 0/07/996 to 30/06/200I. In the 
present case management has assessed age of Pramod Kanu as twenty two years and six months as on [2/03/2007 and 
if said the assessment is considered for the purpose of deciding age of the dependent son then on the death of his 
father, he was thirteen years and eight months of age. According to the provision of clause 9.5.0(ii) name of a male 
dependent has to be maintained in live roster if he is above twelve years of age on the date of death of his father and 
he would be provided employment on attaining age of eighteen years. In the instant case the management has 
committed a clear violation of the provision of NCWA-VI where the management did not take into consideration the 
age of the dependent son for the purpose of maintaining his name in live roster for granting employment. As long as a 
son is a minor and does not have legal competence to decide as to within what time application for employment 
should be submitted, the argument of the management that application for employment was submitted after a long 
delay cannot be accepted. 


9. In the present case management faulted on their part by not providing Monetary Compensation to the wife of 
the deceased though application was filed within one year and eight months. It was the duty of the management to 
extend the benefits of Monetary Compensation and employment to the family of the deceased employee according to 
the terms of settlement. From the evidence of WW-I I find that wife of the deceased, Chandra Kala Devi has died on

6/0/202] as such no Monetary Compensation can be paid to her. Pramod Kanu, dependent son is found eligible and 
entitled to get employment in place of his father in terms of clause 9.5.0(iii) of NCWA-VI. Management of ECL is 
directed to take appropriate step to process the prayer of employment of Pramod Kanu, son of Late Dahu Kanu 
commensurating with his skill and qualification. Management shall complete the process for granting employment to 
the son within one month from date of communication of Award, if the process is not complete within the stipulated 
time, management shall be liable to provide compensation of Rs. 30,000/ per month to the dependent son till 
employment is provided to him. 


Hence, 
ORDERED 


that the Industrial Dispute raised by the union is decided in favour of the petitioner on contest. Management is 
directed to provide employment to Pramod Kanu, son of Late Dahu Kanu within one month from the date of 
communication of Award, in default, management of ECL shall be liable to pay a compensation of Rs. 30,000/ per 
month to the dependent son till employment is provided to him. Let an Award be drawn up in light of my above 
findings and copies of the Award in duplicate be sent to the Ministry for information and Notification.

(Passed on this 0" day of June-2025.) 


As per letter dated 30/09/202 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under section-!0 of I.D. Act, 947 as per reference number L-220/4/202I/IR(CM-I) 
dt. 30/09/202. The dispute under reference related to :- 


“Whether the demand of union of payment of bonus to 88 workers by M/s. Satyawati Services a contractor 
and CM, FCI, Raipur for the year 2076-79 and 2049-20 is legal and justified ? If not, what relief the 88 
workmen, represented through Chhattisgarh Hamal Mazdoor Sangh Rajnandgaon are entitled to ?” 


Notices were sent to the parties after registering a case on the basis of reference. The workman union 
appeared and filed its statement of claim. None appeared for the management of FCI and contractor inspite of service, 
hence case is proceeding ex-parte against them vide order dated 0.0.2024. 


The case of the workman union, as taken by them in their statement of claim is mainly that these workmen, 
mentioned in the Annexure to the Schedule have worked with Food Corporation of India through contractor M/s. 
Satyawati Services in the year 20I8-l9 & 209-20 but were not paid bonus. The union raised a dispute before the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner. After failure of conciliation, reference was sent. The workman union has prayed that 
the workmen be held entitled to get bonus from Food Corporation of India being the principal employer/ the 
contractor. 


None from the side of Food Corporation of India and Contractor appeared. In evidence, the workman union 
has filed affidavit of its General Secretary and affidavit of one worker Basanti Sagar. The union has also filed RTI 
documents with respect to their representation before the Regional Labour Commissioner and conciliation 
proceedings. 


I have heard argument of Mr. R.C. Shrivastava, learned Counsel for the workman union and have gone 
through the record. 


From the uncontroverted affidavits, it is proved that the 88 workmen as per list have worked with Food 


[भागवा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाह़ 2, 947 5079 


Corporation of India as contract workers supplied by the contractor M/s. Satyawati Services. 


Section 2] of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act 970, deals with the responsibility of the 
principal employer (Food Corporation of India in this case), is being reproduced as follows :- 


“20. Liability of principal employer in certain cases.- 


(3) If any amenity required to be provided under Section 76, Section 77, Section 76 or Section 79 for the 
benefit of the contract labour employed in an estab lishment is not provided by the contractor within the 
time prescribed therefore, such amenity shall be provided by the principal employer within such time as 
may be prescribed. 


(2) All expenses incurred by the principal employer in providing the amenity may be recovered by the 
principal employer from the contractor either by deduction from any amount payable to the contractor 
under any contract or as a debt payable by the contractor. 


24. Responsibility for payment of wages.- 


(I) A contractor shall be responsible for payment of wages to each worker employed by him as contract 
labour and such wages shall be paid before the expiry of such period as may be prescribed. 


(2) Every principal employer shall nominate a representative duly authorised by him to be present at the 
time of disbursement of wages by the contractor and it shall be the duty of such representative to certify 
the amounts paid as wages in such manner as may be prescribed. 


(3) It shall be the duty of the contractor to ensure the disbursement of wages in the presence of the 
authorised representative of the principal employer. 


(4) In case the contractor fails to make payment of wages within the prescribed period or makes short 
payment, then the principal employer shall be liable to make payment of wages in full or the unpaid 
balance due, as the case may be, to the contract labour employed by the contractor and recover the 
amount so paid from the contractor either by deduction from any amount payable to the contractor any 
contract as a debt payable by the contractor.” 


From the above referred provision, it is established that the responsibility of payment of wages is of the 
contractor and if he fails to discharge his this responsibility, the principal employer is under obligation to discharge it. 


Now the question arises, as whether bonus is part of wages or not ? 
Section 2(h) of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act 970, defines wages as follows :- 


(h) "wages" shall have the meaning assigned to it in clause (vi) of Section 2 of the Payment of 
Wages Act, 7936 (4 of 7936); 


Section 2(vi) of Payment of Wages Act 936 defines wages as follows:- 


vi) “wages”? means all remuneration (whether by way of salary, allowances, or otherwise) 
expressed in terms of money or capable of being so expressed which would, if the terms of employment, 
express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work 
done in such employment, and includes— 


(a) any remuneration payable under any award or settlement between the parties or order of 
a Court; 


(b) any remuneration to which the person employed is entitled in respect of overtime work or 
holidays or any leave period; 


(c) any additional remuneration payable under the terms of employment (whether called a bonus or 
by any other name); 


(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is payable 
under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum, whether with or without 
deductions, but does not provide for the time within which the payment is to be made; 


(e) any sum to which the person employed is entitled under any scheme framed under any law for 
the time being in force, 


but does not include— 


(3) any bonus (whether under a scheme of profit sharing or otherwise) which does not form part of 
the remuneration payable under the terms of employment or which is not payable under any award or 
settlement between the parties or order of a Court; 


5080 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(2) the value of any house-accommodation, or of the supply of light, water, medical attendance or 
other amenity or of any service excluded from the computation of wages by a general or special order of 
appropriate Government; 


(3) any contribution paid by the employer to any pension or provident fund, and the interest which 
may have accrued thereon; 


(4) any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession; 


(5) any sum paid to the employed person to defray special expenses entailed on him by the nature of 
his employment; or 


(6) any gratuity payable on the termination of employment in cases other than those specified in 
sub-clause (d). 


The relevant provisions with respect to payment of bonus in the Payment of Bonus Act are being 
reproduced as follows :- 


8. Eligibility for bonus.—Every employee shall be entitled to be paid by his employer in an accounting year, 
bonus, in accordance with the provisions of this Act, provided he has worked in the establishment for not less 
than thirty working days in that year. 


9. Disqualification _for_bonus.—Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, an employee shall be 


disqualified from receiving bonus under this Act, if he is dismissed from service for— 
(a) fraud; or 

(b) riotous or violent behaviour while on the premises of the establishment; or 

(c) theft, misappropriation or sabotage of any property of the establishment. 


409. Payment of minimum bonus.—Subject to the other provisions of this Act, every employer shall be bound 
to pay to every employee in respect of the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 7979 and in 
respect of every subsequent accounting year, a minimum bonus which shall be 8.33 per cent. of the salary of 
wage earned by the employee during the accounting year or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher, 
whether or not the employer has any allocable surplus in the accounting year: Provided that where an 
employee has not completed fifteen years of age at the beginning of the accounting year, the provisions of 
this section shall have effect in relation to such employees as if for the words “one hundred rupees”, the 
words “sixty rupees” were substituted. 


44. Payment of maximum bonus.— 


(I) Where in respect of any accounting year referred to in section 709, the allocable surplus exceeds the 
amount of minimum bonus payable to the employees under that section, the employer shall, in lieu of such 
minimum bonus, be bound to pay to every employee in respect of that accounting year bonus which shall be 
an amount in proportion to the salary or wage earned by the employee during the accounting year subject to 
a maximum of twenty per cent. of such salary or wage. 


(2) In computing the allocable surplus under this section, the amount set on or the amount set off under the 
provisions of section ज> shall be taken into account in accordance with the provisions of that section. 


Since, the workman union has not file the terms of contract between the principal employer and contractor, 
has not also filed the terms of engagement between the contractor and its workers, the Food Corporation of India 
cannot be held responsible to pay bonus being a principal employer. Rather, it is the contractor M/s. Satyawati 
Services who are held responsible to pay bonus for the year 20l8-l9 & 209-20 to the workers mentioned in the 
reference. 


On basis of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows :- 
AWARD 


The contractor M/s. Satyawati Services is held responsible to pay bonus for the years 208-9 & 209-20 to 
its contract workers mentioned in the list with interest @ of !0% per annum from the date which the amount of bonus 
became due till the date of payment. 


No order as to cost.

Consider the submission. It appears that the dismissed workman is not inclined to proceed with the case. 
Same is accordingly dismissed for non-prosecution. 


Hence, 
ORDERED

l. File taken up today. The applicant Abid Hasan has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the 


Industrial Disputes Act 947 (hereinafter called the ID Act) to claim reinstatement in service along with arrears of pay 
and allowances with interest. 


2. The brief facts of the case are that the applicant was engaged as on outsider GDS (Gramin Dak Sevak), by 
the Post Master Sub Post Office Darpur on 8.05.203 and rendered a service of one year till 6.05.204 and he was 
retrenched by the respondent without compliance of Section 25F of the ID Act as he had already completed more than 
240 days during the period 6.05.203 to 6.05.204. The applicant filed an application before the Conciliation cum 
Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Karnal in February 20I5, however the conciliation proceedings failed and 
has filed the present application before this Tribunal to seek relief under S 2(A) read with S 25 F,S 25 G and S25 H of 
the ID Act. It is prayed that the status of the applicant be restored and he be granted benefit of service along with 
arrear of pay and allowances along with interest. 


3. Respondent Nos. | & 2 filed written statement alleging therein that the post of GDSMD/C Darpur had fallen 
vacant due to death of Sh. Mohinder Singh GDSMD/C on 30.08.202, who was also holding the charge of GDS BPM 
Darpur due to resignation of the incumbent of the post. Therefore, the work of the GDS BPM was managed by Sh. 
Surjit Singh, GDSMD/C Kot and the work of GDSMD/C Darpur was managed by engaging on Sh. Jaspreet Singh 
outsider. Accordingly, proposal for filling up the post of GDS MD/C Darpur on compassionate grounds was 
forwarded to higher authorities. Till the approval of appointment case on compassionate grounds the work was 
managed by deployment of various outsiders keeping in view the limitations of 89 days at a stretch and 50 days ina 
calendar year. The applicant was engaged to work as outsider as GDS MD/C Darpur to manage the work w.e.f 
6.05.20i3 and as such he worked for the dates as noted below in the year 203 and 20]4. It is further added that 
Branch Postmaster Darpur had engaged the applicant as outsider GDS after approval from ASPOs Yamuna Nagar 
who is appointing authority of the GDS:- 

6-05-203 to 5-06-203, 

7-06-203 to 5-07-203, 

6-07-203 to 0-08-203, 

2-08-203 to 3-08-203 


0-09-203 to 30-09-203 
In the year 204 
0l-0i-204 to 3-0I-204, 
0-02-204 to 28-02-204, 
0-03-204 to 28-03-204 
Total 25 days. 


[भाग ॥---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 5087 


The applicant had not worked after 28.03.204. As the applicant has not worked continuously for 240 days and 
the applicant is not engaged as GDS as such question of giving notice to the applicant does not arise. As regards 
implementation of the provisions of ID Act, it is stated that the Department of Posts is not an industry. Therefore 
provisions of ID Act are not applicable to Department of Posts and its employees. Moreover GDS employees are not 
regular employee working for 8 hours. They are part time employees working for 3 to 5 hours and governed by a 
separate set of Rules called GDS (Conduct and Engagement) Rules, 20l! (hereinafter called as GDS Rules). The 
provisions of the ID Act are not applicable to the Department of Posts and Its employees. Furthermore, the applicant 
was not GDS but was an outsider GDS. It is submitted that the applicant is not entitled for the relief as claimed and 
the application be dismissed with costs. 


Evidence of parties: 


4. In order to prove his case, applicant himself appeared and filed his affidavit Ex.WWI/A along with 
documents Ex.WI to W4 and closed the evidence on behalf of applicant on 3i.0!.2025. Thereafter, respondents have 
examined Sh. Arun Goel, Superintendent of Post Offices, Ambala Division, Ambala, who tendered his affidavit as 
MWI/A along with documents +. ५] & Ex.M2. AR for respondent no.! & 2 closed the evidence on 47.02.2025 and 
the case was fixed for arguments. 


Submissions of Applicant:- 


2. Learned AR of applicant argued orally and contended that the applicant is entitled for the benefits as he has 
claimed in his application and reiterated the claim as stated by him in the application. 


Submissions of respondents:- 


6. Learned AR for respondents contended that the applicant had not worked continuously for 240 days and the 
applicant was not engaged as GDS as such question of giving notice to the applicant does not arise. Moreover GDS 
are governed by a separate set of Rules called GDS Rules. The provisions of the ID Act are not applicable to the 
Department of Posts and its employees. Moreover, the applicant was an outsider GDS and was not even governed by 
GDS Rules. AR for respondents contended that the applicant is not entitled for the relief as claimed and the 
application be dismissed. 


Findings:- 
7. Ihave heard the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


8. It is admitted fact that the applicant Abid Hasan was appointed as an outsider GDS by the Department in 
place of regular incumbent Sh. Mohinder Singh. Outsider GDS are appointed as a stop gap arrangement until regular 
incumbent come on the post. In fact, as per procedure when a GDS appointed by the department is unable to perform 
his duty then as a stop gap arrangement, a temporary arrangement is made until regular incumbent come on that post. 
The substitute appointment is sporadic depending on the period during which the regular is not appointed whatsoever 
reason. Thus, it is clear and proved that applicant rendered his services not an employee of management but as 
nominee of GDS as an outsider. It is also pertinent to mention that as GDS (outsider) is not entitled for any 
termination notice as per GDS Rules. The learned counsel for the applicant could not place any rule before me that 
any notice of termination under the GDS Rules was required before retrenchment by the management of the applicant. 
Moreover, the applicant has also failed to prove that he was appointed on regular basis as GDS, rather applicant was 
appointed as an outsider GDS as stop gap arrangement. He was working as GDS outsider, which are not governed 
under Section 25F of the ID Act. There was no requirement for issuing termination notice as per GDS Rules. 


9. The present application has been filed by the applicant under Section 2A of ID Act, claiming that he was 
retrenched by the management on 6.05.20l4 and he has also approached Conciliation-cum-Assistant Labour 
Commissioner, Karnal during 20l5 and proceedings have failed. Undoubtedly, the applicant covered under ID Act 
can file application under Section 2A of the ID Act against his discharge, dismissal or termination of service after 
failure of the proceedings within 45 days. However, the applicant has not attached any documents that proceedings 
have failed before the conciliation commissioner. Thus, he has directly approach this Court under Section 2A of the 
ID Act, which is not maintainable. Moreover, even if it is presumed that the applicant was covered by the ID Act, 
then it was incumbent upon him to prove that he had worked 240 days in the preceding year from the date of his 
termination, i.e. before 28.03.20l4. However, when the days are counted from !6.05.20I3 to 28.03.20I4, these are 
less than 240 days. On this score also, the application is not maintainable under the ID Act. 


0. Hence, this application under Section 2A is not maintainable and the same is dismissed. File after completion 
be consigned in the record room. Let copy of this award be sent to the Appropriate Government as required under 
Section |7 of the Act for publication.

“ Whether the action of the Management of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. in relation to its / & 2 Incline under 
Jhanjra Area in imposing a punishment of dismissal on Shri Prabir Bouri, Cat-I Mazdoor (Man No. 2469॥,,

| On receiving Order No. L-2202/35/202-IR(CM-ID dated 08.09.202 from the Government of India 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case No. 47 of 202 was registered on 
20.09.202 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing them to appear 
and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims and a list of their 
witnesses. 


2. The workman filed his written statement on 24.07.2023. The fact of the case as disclosed in his written 
statement is that Prabir Bouri, the workman was a permanent employee at Jhanjra Project Colliery under Jhanjra Area 
of Eastern Coalfields Limited (hereinafter referred to as ECL) bearing U.M. No. 74780l. He was appointed on 
9.09.985 and had remained absent from duty from !8.04.20I2 due to his illness. He informed the management 
about the reason of his absence. Despite such information management illegally issued a Charge Sheet to him bearing 
No. AGT/JNR/I&2/P/CS/2/789 dated 30.04.20!2. A Domestic Enquiry was held against him on 24.07.202. The 
workman participated in the Enquiry Proceeding and disclosed the reason of his absence and also submitted Medical 
Certificate in support of his illness. No 2" Show Cause Notice was issued by the management nor any copy of 
Enquiry Proceeding was supplied to him before dismissing him from service, violating the principles of natural 
justice. It is contended that a major punishment has been imposed against the workman, disproportionate to the 
alleged charge. He has been made jobless and forced to a starving condition. The dismissed workman prayed for 
setting aside the order of dismissal, seeking reinstatement in service and payment of back wages.

Prabir Bouri, General Mazdoor, Category — I, was absenting from his duty at Jhanjra Project Colliery since 
8.04.20i2 without any information. A Charge Sheet was issued to Prabir Bouri for misconduct vide Charge Sheet

9. Considered the rival contentions of the union and learned advocate for the management of ECL in light of 
pleading and evidence on record. In the instant case, Kalu Charan Suin was charge sheeted on !2/!2/209 wherein he 
was charged for his unauthorized absence for a period from 6/09/20I9 to 2/I2/209 without information and leave 
and also for his habitual absence from duty. Workman was directed to submit reply within seventy two hours. 
Workman submitted reply to the charge sheet which is produced as Exhibit M-2. In his reply it is submitted that he 
was under medical treatment at Khandra Rural Hospital and again he fell ill from 5/2/209 to 25/02/2020 and was 
unable to join duty. Nowhere in the reply workman stated that after recovery from illness and before issuance of 
charge sheet on 2/I2/209, he had reported to join his duty or was disallowed to join. It is therefore clear that the 
submission made in the written statement that he was disallowed to join duty is untrue and not reliable due to lack of 
evidence and want of consistency. No document relating to illness or medical treatment of the workman has been 
filed along with his reply. Management issued office order dated 04/03/2020 (Exhibit M-3) appointing Shri Ashis 
Mohan, Asstt. Manager (P), Madhabpur colliery to conduct the domestic enquiry. Notice of Enquiry was issued on 
6/03/2020 fixing 2/03/2020 as date for holding domestic enquiry. A copy of Notice of Enquiry is produced as 
Exhibit M-4. It is gathered from the enquiry proceeding (Exhibit M-5) that a domestic enquiry was held against the 
charged employee in respect of charges levelled under clause 26.29 and 26.23 of Certified Standing Orders applicable 
to the company. Content of the charge sheet was explained to the charged employee who understood the charges 
levelled against him. Workman was given opportunity to take assistance of co-workers or representatives of the Trade 
Union but he declined. Management Representatives were examined who clearly gave out that past performance of 
the workman and his attendance from the year 206 to 20I9 appears to be abysmal. It appears that he was warned on 
previous occasions for his unauthorized absence and three increments with cumulative effect were stopped by letter 
dated 2/03/20I5. He was demoted to lower post without any pay protection by letter dated 04/08/20l6 and was 
warned and three increments were stopped with cumulative effect by letter dated 29/ [/207., Workman did not cross- 
examine witnesses and admitted his guilt. It is stated that he suffered from viral fever, liver disorder and pain from 
7/09/209 to 06/2/209 and subsequently from 5/2/209 to 25/02/2020. There is clear admission that he did not 
inform the management nor did he avail any leave. He stated that he submitted medical certificate regarding his 
illness from Khandra (Ukhra) BPHC but in fact no document was submitted before the Enquiry officer nor before the 
Competent Authority of the company. Enquiry Officer held the workman guilty of charges in respect of clause 26.29 
and 26.23 of certified standing orders applicable to the company. A second show cause Notice dated 04/04/2020 was 
issued to the workman (Exhibit M-6) and a copy of enquiry proceeding was enclosed therewith for his perusal. 
Workman replied to the second show cause Notice once again admitting the charge (Exhibit M-7). Competent 
Authority on considering the entire material and reply to the second show cause Notice, dismissed the workman from 
service with effect from 08/05/2020 which was intimated to him in due course of time by way of order of dismissal 
issued by the Agent, Naba Kajora colliery, ECL. 


0. It emerges from the above facts and circumstances that there was no cogent reason to treat the charged 
employee in lenient manner. There was no mitigating circumstance nor any reliable document related to his medical 
treatment, claimed to have been undergone by the workman during the period of his absence. Management of ECL 
has carried out the enquiry proceeding in a proper manner providing reasonable opportunity to the workman to defend 
himself. Principle of Natural Justice has been duly complied in holding the domestic enquiry. A mercy petition has

In this context, reference of few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court are relevant as discussed hereunder:- 


In K RReddy Vs. Industrial Tribunal-II, Hyderabad, Hon’ble Court held:- 


“The Supreme Court extensively considered the scope of relevant provisions and precedent decisions and held that 


there was inordinate, unexplained delay in referring the dispute.’ 


, 


In the case of Assistant Engineer, CAD, Kota and Dhan Kumwar, CA No.6473, 2006 III LLJ, the Hon'ble Apex 
Court have held: 


“workman raising the dispute eight years after termination of service —therefore relief by Labour Court should not 
have been granted to workman.” 


In Haryana State Co-operative Land Development Bank and Neelam, 2005 I LLJ, the Apex Court held: 


“Though no time limit prescribed for raising industrial dispute, but stale claim, could not be entertained - 


approaching Labour Court after delay of more than 7 years. Held:- justified refusal of relief in this case.’ 


, 


In the case of Sri Prabhakar Vs. Joint Director Sericulture Department in Civil Appeal decision dated 7.9.5 
Hon'ble Apex Court have held:- 


“40) On the basis of aforesaid discussion, we summarise the legal position as under: 


“An industrial dispute has to be referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication and the workman 
cannot approach the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal directly, except in those cases which are covered 
by Section 2A of the Act. Reference is made under Section /9 of the Act in those cases where the appropriate 
Government forms an opinion that ‘any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended’. The words ‘industrial 
dispute exists' are of paramount importance unless there is an existence of an industrial dispute (or the dispute 
is apprehended or it is apprehended such a dispute may arise in near future), no reference is to be made. Thus, 
existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is a sine qua non for making the reference. No doubt, at the 
time of taking a decision whether a reference is to be made or not, the appropriate Government is not to go into 
the merits of the dispute. Making of reference is only an administrative function. At the same time, on the basis 
of material on record, satisfaction of the existence of the industrial dispute or the apprehension of an industrial 
dispute is necessary. Such existence/apprehension of industrial dispute, thus, becomes a condition precedent, 
though it will be only subjective satisfaction based on material on record. Since, we are not concerned with the 
satisfaction dealing with cases where there is apprehended industrial dispute, discussion that follows would 
confine to existence of an industrial dispute. Dispute or difference arises when one party make a demand and 
other party rejects the same. It is held by this Court in number of cases that before raising the industrial dispute 
making of demand is a necessary pre-condition. In such a scenario, if the services of a workman are terminated 
and he does not make the demand and/or raise the issue alleging wrongful termination immediately thereafter 
or within reasonable time and raises the same after considerable lapse of period, whether it can be said that 
industrial dispute still exist. Since there is no period of limitation, it gives right to the workman to raise the 
dispute even belatedly. However, if the dispute is raised after a long period, it has to be seen as to whether such 
a dispute still exists? Thus, notwithstanding the fact that law of limitation does not apply, it is to be shown by 
the workman that there is a dispute in praesenti. For this purpose, he has to demonstrate that even if 
considerable period has lapsed and there are laches and delays, such delay has not resulted into making the 
industrial dispute seized to exist. Therefore, if the workman is able to give satisfactory explanation for these 
laches and delays and demonstrate that the circumstances discloses that issue is still alive, delay would not 
come in his way because of the reason that law of limitation has no application. On the other hand, if because 
of such delay dispute no longer remains alive and is to be treated as “dead”, then it would be non-existent 
dispute which cannot be referred. Take, for example, a case where the workman issues notice after his 
termination, questioning the termination and demanding reinstatement. He is able to show that there were 
discussions from time to time and the parties were trying to sort out the matter amicably. Or he is able to show 
that there were assurances by the Management to the effect that he would be taken back in service and because 
of these reasons, he did not immediately raise the dispute by approaching the labour authorities seeking 
reference or did not invoke the remedy under Section 2A of the Act. In such a scenario, it can be treated that the 
dispute was live and existing as the workman never abandoned his right. However, in this very example, even if 
the notice of demand was sent but it did not evoke any positive response or there was specific rejection by the 
Management of his demand contained in the notice and thereafter he sleeps over the matter for number of 
years, it can be treated that he accepted the factum of his termination and rejection thereof by the Management 
and acquiesced into the said rejection. Take another example. A workman approaches the Civil Court by filing 
a suit against his termination which was pending for number of years and was ultimately dismissed on the 
ground that Civil Court did not have jurisdiction to enforce the contract of personal service and does not grant 
any reinstatement. At that stage, when the suit is dismissed or he withdraws that suit and then involves the 
machinery under the Act, it can lead to the conclusion that dispute is still alive as the workman had not 
accepted the termination but was agitating the same; albeit in a wrong forum. In contrast, in those cases where 
there was no agitation by the workman against his termination and the dispute is raised belatedly and the delay 


[भाग Il—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 53 


or laches remain unexplained, it would be presumed that he had waived his right or acquiesced into the act of 
termination and, therefore, at the time when the dispute is raised it had become stale and was not an ‘existing 
dispute’. In such circumstances, the appropriate Government can refuse to make reference. In the alternative, 
the Labour Court/Industrial Court can also hold that there is no “industrial dispute” within the meaning 
of Section 2(k) of the Act and, therefore, no relief can be granted. 


447) We may hasten to clarify that in those cases where the Court finds that dispute still existed, though raised 
belatedly, it is always permissible for the Court to take the aspect of delay into consideration and mould the 
relief. In such cases, it is still open for the Court to either grant reinstatement without back wages or lesser 
back wages or grant compensation instead of reinstatement. We are of the opinion that the law on this issue has 
to be applied in the aforesaid perspective in such matters.” 


Moreover, in the case of Chief Engineer (Construction) Vs. Keshav Rao, 2005 JCR 96, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held that, the delay of a one year and five months in issuing a notice appears to us to be significant. Here, in the 
present matter workman has not issued any notice or raised dispute against his termination in any forum for a long 
period of about fourteen years and his claim against dismissal has become stale due to inordinate delay and latches.

charge levelled against the delinquent Workman, Disciplinary Authority has passed the order to dismiss the 
Workman from service of the company with effect from 29.!.998. Therefore, in view of the above the order of 
dismissal of the Workman from service does not suffer from any procedural infirmity or illegality or perversity. 


3. Although, Petitioner workman has taken the plea that due to his sickness and other family problems he 
could not be regular to his duties during the year !997, thus, he also admitted the absent period during the year 997 
as alleged in the chargesheet. As per chargesheet he had put in only I8 days of attendance during the year 4997 and 
this fact has been admitted by the Workman in his statement recorded during the enquiry. But he has not submitted 
any document in evidence in support of his plea that he was regularly ill during the absence period and he has gone 
under treatment for the illness. Further, he failed to furnish any explanation that why he did not intimate about his 
absence to the Respondent management and also why he did not report sickness at the Respondent’s hospital. 
Therefore, for the want of any evidence in support of the plea, argument of the Petitioner workman of illness is not 
tenable. He has taken the plea that he could not attend his duty during the year !997 due to ill-health. Whereas the 
chargesheet dated 25.9.998 was issued to the Workman for conducting the enquiry for unauthorized absence from 
duty during the year 997. Further, the record of enquiry proceeding goes to reveal that the Workman was served 
with chargesheet and documents and he participated in the enquiry at every stage of proceedings. He was also 
accorded the opportunity to cross examine witness but he did not avail it. Therefore, the plea of the Petitioner 
workman that the termination order has been passed by Respondent in violation of principles of natural justice is not 
tenable. Thus, the said plea of Workman is not tenable. 


4. In this context, the reference of decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court are relevant wherein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have held that, the misconduct of habitual absence from duty unauthorisedly by the employee is a 
serious and grave nature. 


In State of U.P. V. Ashok Kumar Singh 996 () SCC 302, wherein the Apex Court had held:- 


“Having notices the fact that the first Respondent has absented himself from duty without level on several occasions, 
we are unable to appreciate the High Court's observation that ‘his absence from duty would not amount to such a 
grave charge. Even otherwise on the facts of this case, there was no justification for the High Court to interfere with 
the punishment holding that 'the punishment does not commensurate with the gravity of the charge’ especially when 
the High Court concurred with the findings of the Tribunal on facts. No case for interference with the punishment is 
made out.” 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाह़ 2, 947 55 


In the case of North Eastern Karnataka R.T. Corpn. v. Ashappa decided on 2 May, 2006 wherein, the Apex 
Court had held:- 


“Remaining absent for a long time, in our opinion, cannot be said to be a minor misconduct. The Appellant 
runs a fleet of buses. It is a statutory organization. It has to provide public utility services. For running the 
buses, the service of the conductor is imperative. No employer running a fleet of buses can allow an employee 
to remain absent for a long time. The Respondent had been given opportunities to resume his duties. Despite 
such notices, he remained absent. He was found not only to have remained absent for a period of more than 
three years, his leave records were seen and it was found that he remained unauthorisedly absent on several 
occasions. In this view of the matter, it cannot be said that the misconduct committed by the Respondent herein 
has to be treated lightly. 


In Delhi Transport Corporation v. Sardar Singh [(2004) 7 SCC 574], the Apex Court held-: 


"II. Conclusions regarding negligence and lack of interest can be arrived at by looking into the period of 
absence, more particularly, when same is unauthorised. Burden is on the employee who claims that there was 
no negligence and/or lack of interest to establish it by placing relevant materials. Clause (ii) of para 4 of the 
Standing Orders shows the seriousness attached to habitual absence. In clause (i) thereof, there is requirement 
of prior permission. Only exception made is in case of sudden illness. There also conditions are stipulated, non- 
observance of which renders the absence unauthorised." 


State of U.P. v. Sheo Shanker Lal Srivastava and Others [(2006) 3 SCC 276], 


it was opined that, “the Industrial Courts or the High Courts would not normally interfere with the quantum of 
punishment imposed upon by the Respondent stating: "It is now well-settled that principles of law that the High 
Court or the Tribunal in exercise of its power of judicial review would not normally interfere with the quantum 
of punishment. Doctrine of proportionality can be invoked only under certain situations. It is now well-settled 
that the High Court shall be very slow in interfering with the quantum of punishment unless it is found to be 
shocking to one's conscience." 


The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Management Coal India Ltd. v. Mukul Kumar Choudhary Civil Appeal 
5762-5763 of 2009 decided on 24.08.2009 laid down the test of proportionality of punishment and held:- 


“One of the test to be applied while dealing with the question of punishment would be: would any reasonable 
employer have imposed such punishment in like circumstances? Obviously, a reasonable employer is expected 
to take into consideration measure, magnitude and degree of misconduct and all other relevant circumstances 
and exclude irrelevant matters before imposing punishment.” 


In the case of Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation Vs. Dilip Uttam Jayabhay, the 2022 LLR page 
26, wherein the Hon’ble Apex Court held:- 


“once the enquiry finding is held to be fair and proper, industrial Tribunal or Labour Court lacks jurisdiction to 
interfere with the quantum of punishment unless the same is shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of conduct.” 


Therefore, in view of the fore gone discussion and a law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court I am of the considered 
opinion that the dismissal order passed by the Respondent management was proportionate and commensurate with the 
gravity of the charges hence deserves to be upheld. There is no illegality or impropriety or perversity in the 
impugned order. 


This issue is decided against the Workman and in favour of the Respondent. 


5. Issue No.IV:- In view of the finding given at Issue Nos. I , II and III the Workman is not entitled for any 
relief, hence the petition is liable to be dismissed. 


This issue is answered accordingly. 
AWARD 


In view of discussion and finding arrived at Issues No. I, II & II, the action of the General Manager, M/s. 
Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., Ramagundam-I Area, Godavrikhani, Karimnagar Distt., in terminating the 
services of Sri Akula Odelu, Ex. Coal Filler, GDK-I Inc., RG-I Area with effect from 29..998 is held justified. 
The workman is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. Therefore, the claim petition is dismissed as devoid of 
merits. Reference is answered accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

l. This is an application U/S 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act (here in after referred as an “Act”) for

Whether the termination of the services of the applicants w.e.f 09.03.20l0 by the Medical Superintendent,

2. Claimants namely Sh. Swatantra Kumar, Mohd. Yusuf, Vinod Kumar, Mahesh Kumar and Rita Kumari had stated in 
the claim statement that they were appointed with the management as Nursing Attendant on daily wage basis at the 
rate of Rs. 4440+300 Grade Pay per month plus D.A since .2.2009. 


3. They were initially appointed as daily wage workers through a regular advertisement in Employment News, with 
pay aligned to the standard group- D scale for the position. Since 984, the policy of the hospital had been to 
regularize eligible casual workers into permanent posts. On !2.09.2007, the hospital wrote to the DG Health Services 
requesting the regularization of 2] casual workers. 


4. On 7.03.2008, the hospital informed that it had 25 sanctioned daily wage positions, with 86 workers granted 
temporary status after one year of service, and requested regularization for the remaining workers due to the high 
patient to nurse ratio and the technical nature of the Nursing Attendant posts. The respondents regularly regularized 
daily wage workers, including nursing attendants, as per the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) letter 
dated 29.2.2008. On 24.3.2008, 47 daily wage workers were regularized with a monthly pay of Rs. 2550/- in the pay 
scale of Rs. 2550-3200 and other allowances. On .6.2008, Respondent No.3 raised concerns about outsourcing 
nursing attendants, citing issues with suitability, accountability, and control over outsourced workers. On .6.2009, 
Respondent No.3 informed the Ministry of Health that the hospital had 25 daily wage workers, who were regularly 
appointed through proper procedures, including interviews, advertisements, and employment exchange processes. 
They requested permission to continue the 70 daily wage workers until they were regularized. 


5. On 26.6.2009, Respondent No.3 wrote to the Ministry of Health, highlighting a critical shortage of !50 nursing 
attendants at the hospital due to the sanctioned strength not being raised since [989, and requested an extension of the 
daily wage appointments for the applicants. As a result, their services were extended until 26.4.200. 


6. On 23.0.2009, Respondent No.3 again requested Respondent No.2 to expedite the approval for outsourcing 50 
nursing attendants and regularizing 70 daily wage attendants after the superannuation of existing Group D employees. 
However, Respondent No.2 did not respond. On 3..2009, Respondent No.2 instructed the publication of a tender 
for outsourcing 70 nursing attendants. On 7..2009, Respondent No.3 informed Respondent No.2 about the 
published tender and requested the regularization of 70 daily wage nursing attendants. Their termination is unlawful, 
arbitrary, and violates the hospital's own policies and Sections 25F, 25G, and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
947, as they worked over 240 days. They had gone to the conciliation officer, but, it was resulted into failure. Hence, 
they have filed the present claim. 


‘th WS had been filed by the management on 02.07.204. He denied the averment made in the claim statement. He 
also submitted that present application is liable to be dismissed. 


8. After completion of the proceedings, following issues have been framed on 3.0.204 i.e.- 


(i) Whether the termination of workmen on 09.03.20l0 by management is in violation of Section 25F, G 
& H of the LD Act of 947? If so its effects? 


(i) | Whether workmen are entitled for regularization as they perform duties for period more than 240 days 
preceding their termination? If so its effects? 


(iii) | Whether employee and employer relationship exists between management and workmen? If so its 
effects? 
(iv) To what relief workmen/claimants are entitled? 
9. Evidence of WWl, WW2, WW3 and WW4 i.e. Swatantra Kumar, Mohd. Yusuf, Vinod Kumar, Mahesh Kumar 


and Rita Kumari and ५७४] i.e. Sh. Asharam Meena have been concluded and their examination have also been done. 
Now, the matter is listed for argument. 


0. I have heard the argument on behalf of both the parties at bar. At that time of argument, this tribunal found that 
this claim petition was filed by the claimants in the year 204, much beyond the period of limitation prescribed U/s 2- 
A (3). Before we proceed further, it is necessary to produce the text of section 2-A: 


“2-A. Dismissal, etc., of an individual workman to be deemed to be an industrial dispute.- [(l)] where any 
employer discharges, dismisses, retrenches, or otherwise terminates the services of an individual workman, any 


58 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


dispute or difference between that workman and his employer connected with, or arising out of such discharge, 
dismissal, retrenchment or termination shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute not withstanding that no 
other workman nor any union of workmen is a party to the dispute. 


(2) Not withstanding anything contained in section 709, any such workman as is specified in sub-section (/) may, 
make an application direct to the Labour Court or Tribunal for adjudication of the dispute referred to therein 
after the expiry of forty-five days from the date he has made the application to the Conciliation Officer of the 
appropriate Government for conciliation of the dispute, and in receipt of such application the Labour Court or 
Tribunal shall have powers and jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the dispute, as if it were a dispute referred to it 
by the appropriate Government in accordance with the provisions of this act and all the provisions of this act 
shall apply in relation to such adjudication as they apply in relation to an industrial dispute referred to it by the 
appropriate Government. 


(3) The application referred to in sub-section (2) shall be made to the Labour Court or Tribunal before the 
expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or otherwise termination of service as 
specified in sub-section (4). 


l.A perusal of the aforesaid section would go to show that a dispute connected with or arising out of discharge, 
dismissal, retrenchment or otherwise termination of services of the workman can be directly agitated by workman 
U/s 2-A of the act and it is not necessary that such dispute should be sponsored by the trade union or a substantial 
number of workmen. However, what is required is that workman who has been discharged, dismissed, retrenched or 
terminated as specified in sub-section () of section 2-A can make an application directly to Labour Court or Tribunal 
for adjudication of his individual dispute after expiry of 45 days from the date he has made an application to 
conciliation officer of appropriate government for conciliation of dispute. Sub-section 3 of section 2-A lay down the 
time limit for making such application to Labour Court or the tribunal. It provides that such application to Labour 
Court or tribunal shall be made before expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or 
otherwise termination of services as specified in sub-section-|. This right is available to the workman without any 
effect upon remedy available in section |0 of the act. 


2. Here admittedly, workmen had filed the claim in the year 204 after more than 4 years of their termination which is 
beyond the prescribed limit for filing the claim U/s 2(A) of the I.D Act. Hence, claim petition stands dismissed.

U/s 7 of the I.D Act. File is consigned to record room.

"(s) “workman means any person employed (including an apprentice) in any industry to do any skilled or 
unskilled manual or clerical work for hire or reward and includes, for the purposes of any proceeding under
