or the running out of the stipulated term. To protect the weak against the strong this policy of comprehensive 
definition has been effectuated. Termination embraces not merely the act of termination by the employer, but 
the fact of termination howsoever produced. Maybe, the present may be a hard case, but we can visualize 


abuses by employers, by suitable verbal devices, circumventing the armor of Section 25-F and Section 2(00). 


Without speculating on possibilities, we may agree that "retrenchment" is no longer terra incognita but area 


covered by an expansive definition. It means "to end, conclude, cease" 


(see also Punjab Land Development And _ Reclaimation Corporation Ltd., Chandigarh _y. Presiding Officer 
Labour Court, Chandigarh (7990) 3 SCC 682.) 


Reverting to the facts of the present case and from the documents which are filed on behalf of workman mentioned 
hereinabove and again quoted below:- 
i) Photocopy of documents towards payment made to the applicant & other documents for the period 


25.5.995 till December 995 during which he had worked; 


ii) Photocopy of documents towards payment made to the applicant & other documents for the period 
January 996 to December [996 during which he had worked; 


iii) Photocopy of documents towards payment made to the applicant, salary register & other documents 
for the period January 997 to December 997 during which he had worked; 


iv) Photocopy of documents towards payment made to the applicant, salary register & other documents 
for the period January 998 to October 998 during which he had worked; 


v) Photocopy of representation dated !3.3.2006 submitted by the applicant to the Employer for his 
reinstatement. 


And from the other materials placed by the parties on record, it clearly established that the workman failed to prove 
and establish that he has worked continuously 240 days in the last preceding calendar year, so the relief as claimed by 
the applicant regarding his retrenchment of service, cannot be granted in view of the points as stated hereinabove and 
the law as laid down by the Hon’ble Gauhati High Court in the case of Binay Kumar Singh Versus State Bank of 
India reported in 2024 (762) FLR 78 and the Hon’ble Himanchal Pradesh High Court in the case of Rakesh 
Sharma Versus Indian Oil Corporation reported in 20224(782) FLR 89. 


544 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Order 
For the foregoing reasons the applicant is not entitled for the reliefs as claimed by him in the present I.D. Case, hence, 
the claim of the applicant Sri Triloki Nath Yadav is hereby dismissed. The reference is answered accordingly. 
Award as above.

2: The averments made is the claim statement are as follows: 

It is submitted that, the concerned workman was appointed in the year 983 as Badli Filler and by virtue of his hard 
work and sincerity, he was confirmed as Coal Filler and later promoted as Trammer. While the workman was 
working a Trammer at KTK-I Incline. a charge sheet dt.27-06-2005 was issued alleging that having booked IN 
muster on 27-06-2005, he did not go to distribution point and instigated other workman not to go to distribution point 
which resulted in illegal strike. On receipt of the above charge sheet workman has submitted his reply on 30-06-2005 
not only denying the charge, but also explained all the factual aspects. However, without considering of any of the 
submissions made by the concerned workman, an enquiry was initiated in a pre-determined manner. During the 
enquiry, the concerned workman was not afforded any opportunity, much less valid in nature. It is submitted that, the 
enquiry officer, the presenting officer and all others know pretty well that, the concerned workman was an illiterate 
and more specifically he is not aware of English language. As per the circulars issued by the Management, the 
enquiry has to be conducted in the language known to the workman and has to be explained before commencement of 
enquiry. However, in the instant case, neither the procedure of enquiry was explained nor the proceedings of enquiry 
drafter in the language known to the concerned workman. Having typed the proceedings of enquiry in English and 
the signatures of the concerned workman were obtained without even explaining the contents. As a result of the 
above, the concerned workman was put to great prejudice which resulted in imposing of penalty. It is submitted that 
during the enquiry, the workman was neither provided the opportunity to lead the evidence nor he was permitted to 
cross examine the management witnesses. In fact, the concerned workman was not made aware of the fact that he can 
avail the services of a defense assistant. As a result of above improper conduct of enquiry, the concerned workman 
put to great prejudice which resulted in issuance of order of punishment. It is submitted that the charge alleged against 
the workman itself is not correct, as, the management witness cited the name of the concerned workman, he was 
implicated in this false case. In fact, the concerned workman need not be present at the common distribution point 
being conducted by the management witness. Without application of mind, though the concerned workman was not 
responsible for the charge, he was treated as delinquent and by conducting a farce enquiry he was imposed with a 
penalty, which is incorrect. As a matter of fact, leaving the other workman, who did not respond to his call, the 
management witness quoted workman’s name and the disciplinary proceedings were initiated against the concerned 
workman on a pick and choose method. The above action on the part of the Respondents is not only unjustifiable but 
also discriminatory in nature. As a matter of fact, the concerned workman was directed to work as Jig Trammer at 24 
Dip District of 3 Seam. The concerned workman along with other Trammers went underground to carry out their 
duties as Trammer. The Trammers were not at all on strike whereas the coal fillers were on strike. Therefore, the 


workman, though narrated all the above factual aspects, which were remained unrebutted during the course of 


550 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
enquiry, despite, enquiry officer came to a perverse conclusion that, the charge alleged against the concerned 
workman was held proved. It is no more a res integra that, the enquiry officer should act like a judge and he cannot 
act like a representative of the management. Further, it is the bounden duty of the enquiry officer to analyze the 
evidence on record and come to an independent conclusion without being influenced by either the presenting officer 
or by any other management representatives. | However, in the instant case, the enquiry officer acted like a 
representative of the management and proceeded with a preconceived notion, as if, the concerned workman is guilty 
of charge. A bare perusal of findings of the enquiry officer clearly establish that, they are the outside the scope of 
proceedings of enquiry. It is submitted that though the presenting officer relied upon several documents to hold the 
concerned workman as guilty, none of those documents were shown or furnished to the concerned workman before or 
during the course of enquiry. Even the presenting officer has submitted those documents after the conclusion of 
evidence of the workman and exclusively relying upon those documents, enquiry officer came to a perverse 
conclusion that the concerned workman is guilty of charge. Further, it is submitted that though the strict rules of 
evidence are not applicable to the departmental enquiries, but the departmental enquiries cannot be treated as mere 
sham, more specifically when the civil rights of the delinquent employees are being deprived, such as reduction of 
pay. It is submitted that the charge alleged against the concerned workman was the he instigated other workman to 
go on strike on 27.6.2005. However, there is no evidence to support the charge alleged. Simply because, the 
management witness stated that the concerned workman did not stop the other workman of 3 Seam from going on 
illegal strike, it cannot be treated as misconduct. With great respect, the appreciation of evidence of record by the 
enquiry officer is absolutely hopeless and perverse in nature. Instigating the workmen to go on strike is different 
than not stopping the workmen from going on illegal strike. It is submitted that while deposing before the enquiry 
officer, the management witness never stated that he gave a complaint to the management on 27.6.2005. Even in the 
charge sheet, there was no indication about the alleged complaint. No such document was either pleaded or filed 
before the enquiry officer till the deposition of the workman. As the enquiry officer has relied upon the said 
document and the impugned order was issued basing on such perverse findings of the enquiry officer, penalty 
imposed on the concerned workman is liable to be set aside and all the increments deferred are liable to be restored 
back along with all consequential benefits. It is submitted that the enquiry officer refers to loss of 340 tonnes of coal 
worth Rs.3,39,520/- on 27.6.2005 in 3 shifts, there was no evidence to that extent during the enquiry. Having 
permitted the presenting officer to submit the documents after conclusion of deposition by the concerned workman, 
the enquiry officer erroneously concludes that "since there is no denial from the workman in this regard and the 
document submitted by the Presenting Officer to the effect that SCCL Company was declared as Public Utility 


service and participation in the strike is prohibited vide Cir. No. CRP/Per/IR/E/ISI/357 dt. 05/07.03.05, and also the 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 55] 
Telugu version, which was also displayed on Notice board of the Mine on 3.03.05 and also Form 'N' and Form C' 
regarding commencement and termination of the strike held from 27.06.05 to 29.06.05 have also been sent to the 
authorities concerned and also a charge sheeted employee confirmed he had also participated in the strike". The above 
findings of the enquiry officer are wholly perverse in nature. The penalty imposed on the concerned workman 
basing on such perverse findings is liable to be set aside. Be that as it may, the impugned office order 
No.BHP/PER/20-D/4053 dated 3.0.2007 issued by the Respondent imposing the punishment of reversion to a 
lower stage by reducing four increments/SPRAS in the present scale of pay with effect from |..2007 with 
cumulative effect is without any basis. The impugned order passed by the Respondent is cryptic and does not 
disclose any reasons, much less valid in nature. It is to humbly submit that any order which affects the civil the 
rights of the employees should contain the reasons. In the instant case, impugned order does not contain any reasons. 
Therefore, the impugned order is liable to be set aside on this ground alone. It is submitted that aggrieved by the 
above penalty imposed by the Respondent, the workman approached the Respondent requesting to restore the 
increments as he was implicated in the above false case. However, when nothing resulted positively, he has

[भाग Il—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 559 
As regards jurisdiction of Tribunal to interfere in the finding of the Enquiry Officer, Hon'ble Supreme Court in the 


case of State of Rajasthan vs. Heem Singh, Civil Appeal No.3340 of 2020 dt.29.0.202 have held as hereunder:- 


“33. In exercising judicial review in disciplinary matters, there are two ends of the spectrum. The first embodies a 
rule of restraint. The second defines when interference is permissible. The rule of restraint constricts the ambit of 
judicial review. This is for a valid reason. The determination of whether a misconduct has been committed lies 
primarily within the domain of the disciplinary authority. The judge does not assume the mantle of the disciplinary 
authority. Nor does the judge wear the hat of an employer. Deference to a finding of fact by the disciplinary authority 
is a recognition of the idea that it is the employer who is responsible for the efficient conduct of their service. 
Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof beyond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy — deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. At the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. A failure to consider vital evidence is an incident of what 
the law regards as a perverse 


PART J determination of fact. Proportionality is an entrenched feature of our jurisprudence. Service jurisprudence 
has recognized it for long years in allowing for the authority of the court to interfere when the finding or the penalty 
are disproportionate to the weight of the evidence or misconduct. Judicial craft lies in maintaining a steady sail 
between the banks of these two shores which have been termed as the two ends of the spectrum. Judges do not rest 
with a mere recitation of the hands-off mantra when they exercise judicial review. To determine whether the finding 
in a disciplinary enquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of scrutiny is undertaken. That is to 
satisfy the conscience of the court that there is some evidence to support the charge of misconduct and to guard 
against perversity. But this does not allow the court to re-appreciate evidentiary findings in a disciplinary enquiry or 
to substitute a view which appears to the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would offend the first principle 
which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense without which the judges’ 
craft is in vain.” 


Further in the case of Roop Singh Negi vs. Punjab National Bank & Ors. On 9.2.2008, AIR 2008 SC92I, 


Hon'ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“॥2, In Moni Shankar v. Union of India and Anr. [(2008) 3 SCC 484], this Court held: 


7. The departmental proceeding is a quasi judicial one. Although the provisions of the Evidence Act are not 
applicable in the said proceeding, principles of natural justice are required to be complied with. The Court exercising 
power of judicial review are entitled to consider as to whether while inferring commission of misconduct on the part 
of a delinquent officer relevant piece of evidence has been taken into consideration and irrelevant facts have been 
excluded therefrom. Inference on facts must be based on evidence which meet the requirements of legal principles. 
The Tribunal was, thus, entitled to arrive at its own conclusion on the premise that the evidence adduced by the 
department, even if it is taken on its face value to be correct in its entirety, meet the requirements of burden of proof, 
namely - 


preponderance of probability. If on such evidences, the test of the doctrine of proportionality has not been satisfied, 
the Tribunal was within its domain to interfere. We must place on record that the doctrine of unreasonableness is 
giving way to the doctrine of proportionality." 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court as discussed above, this court has got jurisdiction 


to interfere in the perverse finding of the Enquiry Officer as well as the Disciplinary Authority. 


Further, in the case of Workmen of Food Corporation of India vs. Union of India 997 II LLJ 462 Calcutta High 
Court Hon'ble High Court have held:- 


“II. In the Gujarat Steel Tubes Mazdoor Sabha (supra), the Supreme Court held that mere participation in a strike 
which has been declared illegal cannot by itself be said to be a misconduct to justify an order of dismissal. In this 


560 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


decision the Supreme Court quoted with approval its earlier decision in Indian General Navigation and Railway Co. 
Ltd. v. Their Workmen, (7969-7-7./.08 3) wherein it was held that even in case where the strike was declared illegal 
affecting a public utility service, the "only question of practical importance which may arise would be the kind or 
quantum of punishment and that, of course, has to be modulated in accordance with the facts and circumstances of 
each case ...... there may be reasons for distinguishing of the case of those who may have acted as mere dumb-driven 
cattle from those who have taken an active part in fomenting the trouble and instigating the workmen to join such a 
strike, or have taken recourse to violence." 


42. To determine the question of punishment a clear distinction has to be made between those workmen who not only 
joined in such a strike, but also took part in obstructing the loyal workmen from carrying on their work, or took part 
in violent demonstration, or acted in defiance of law and order, on the one hand and those workmen who are more or 
less silent participators in such a strike, on the other. It is not in the interest of industry that there should be a 
wholesale dismissal of all the workmen who merely participated in such a strike. It is certainly not in the interest of 
the workmen themselves. An Industrial Tribunal, therefore, has to consider the question of punishment keeping in 
view the overriding consideration of the full and efficient working of the industry as a whole. Section IIA of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 947 lays down that where an Industrial Dispute relating to discharge or dismissal has been 
referred to a Tribunal for adjudication and in the course of the adjudication proceeding the Tribunal is satisfied that 
the order of the discharge or dismissal was not justified, it may by its award set aside the order of the discharge or 
dismissal and direct reinstatement of the workman on certain terms, if any as it may think or may give such other 
relief to the workman including awarding a lesser punishment in lieu of discharge or dismissal as the circumstances 
may require.” 


6. Therefore, in view of fore gone discussion and law laid down by Hon'ble Court as discussed above, the 
finding of the Enquiry Officer that the CSE has committed misconduct of participating in illegal strike or instigated 
the other Workmen to commit the strike is illegal and perverse for want of relevant evidence and same is not 
sustainable. Further, the findings of the Enquiry Officer regarding the loss of output to the tune of 343 tonns due to 
the alleged participation of the CSE Workman in the strike is also without any basis and rationale, and the same is 
not sustainable in the eye of law. Therefore, I am of the view that the punishment order passed by the Disciplinary 
Authority in respect of the Petitioner Workman for imposition of reversion by 4 increments/SPRAs with cumulative 
effect to him is liable to be set aside. Hence, the action of the Respondent management in awarding punishment of 
reversion to a lower stage by reducing four increments/SPRAs in the present scale of pay w.e.f. l.!.2007 is not 
justified. 


This point is answered in favour of the Workman and against the Respondent. 


7. Issue No.II: In view of the fore gone discussion and finding arrived at Issue No.I, this Court is of considered 
view that the finding of the enquiry officer holding the Workman guilty of the charges under Company’s Standing 
Order No. 25. l, 25.6, 25.24 is illegal and not justifiable. Therefore, the finding of the Enquiry Officer holding 
the petitioner as guilty of the aforesaid charges is liable to be set aside and consequently the order dated |..2007 
passed by Disciplinary Authority passed against the petitioner Sri Pantangi Rajam, Trammer of imposition of 
punishment of reversion to a lower stage by reducing four increments/ SPRAS in the present scale of pay with 
cumulative effect is liable to be set aside. 


This Issue is decided in favour of the Workman and against the Respondent. 
AWARD 


In the result, the claim petition is allowed. The punishment order No. BHP/PER/20-d/4053 dated 3.0.2007 
passed by General Manager, M/s. Singareni Collieries Co. Ltd., whereby punishment of reversion to a lower stage by 
reducing four increments/ SPRAS in the present scale of pay with cumulative effect has been imposed upon 
Petitioner Sri Panthangi Rajam, Trammer w.e.f. .!.2007 is hereby set aside. The Respondent management is 
directed to restore the increments of Sri Panthangi Rajam, Trammer, from the date of the order of punishment, 
i.e.,l..2007, within one month from the receipt of this award. The Reference is answered accordingly. 


Award passed accordingly. Transmit.

The applicant workman has filed this petition under Section 2-A (2&3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
947, hereinafter referred by the word ‘Act’, with a case that he was engaged by the Branch Manager of Khachrod 
Branch Ujjain in July, 998 for different intervals as a Daily Wager for cleaning of the Branch and was engaged on 
5.07.2006 by the Branch Manager of the Branch on the post of Office Peon and cleaning under his orders. He 
worked eight hours a day continuously till the day of termination on 22.03.206 by the Management Bank. He further 
alleged that the Bank started recruitment process for the post of cleaner/peon. He also submitted an application being 
a Daily Wager in the process. He was called for interview by Management Bank, vide its letter dated 3!.0.20l4 
which was scheduled on 4..204. He did appear in the interview, but was not selected. 


According to the Applicant Workman, he was paid any compensation or notice by those in his 
disengagement is in violation of Section 25F and 25G of the Act. The workman has thus prayed that, holding his 
disengagement against law, he be held entitled to be reinstated with back wages and benefits. 


In its written reply to the petition, the Management has taken a case that he was not a regularly appointed 
employee following recruitment process rather he was a Daily Wager who was called for work on as and when 
required basis. He never worked continuously for 240 days in any year. Being a daily wager who had worked with the 
Bank for few days, he was called for interview for the post of Peon cum Cleaner in the recruitment process held in 
203-4, but could not be selected. Thereafter, he was never engaged by Management Bank. Management has prayed 
the dismissal of his petition. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed Photocopy documents which he has proved as Exhibit W-l to W-22. 
These documents will be referred to as and when required. 


The Workman has further filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief; he has been cross-examined by 
the Management. 


The Management has filed affidavit of its witness Vijay Kumar Maheswari as his examination-in-chief. He 
was not produced for cross-examination. Management filed affidavit of another witness Prakash Laxman Kewal 
Ramani, as his examination-in-chief. He was cross-examined by Workman. Management has filed and proved 
documents relating to recruitment in 203.4, to be referred to as and when require. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for Applicant Workman Shri Arun Patel and Learned Counsel for 
Management Bank Shri Neeraj Kewat. I have gone through the record as well. 


From the perusal of record in the light of rival arguments it comes out that on the basis of being engaged 
by Management Bank as a daily wager he was given an opportunity in the recruitment process held in 203-4, and 
he did appeared in that process, but cannot be selected. There is no dispute between the parties with regard to this 
factual position. According to the Applicant Workman, the recruitment process was vitiated as it was mala fide or 
there where irregularities but this process is not challenged before this Tribunal, hence it is not a subject matter of 
dispute. 


Case of the Workman is that, he continued to work even after he was not selected in the recruitment 
process, and he worked till 22.03.20l6 when his services were terminated by Management without notice or 
compensation as alleged by the Applicant Workman. Management has denied this allegation; hence the burden to 
proof his continuous appointment from date of closer of recruitment process till date of his alleged disengagement is 
on Workman. 


Section 25B of the Act requires to be reproduced here and is being reproduced as follows:- 


25B. Definition of continuous service — 


(7) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in 
uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or 
authorised leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out or a cessation of 
work which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause () for a period 
of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an 
employer— 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar months 
preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually 
worked under the employer for not less than — 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below ground 
in a mine; and 


[भाग Il—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाह़ 2, 947 563 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


(b) for a period of six months, if the workman, during a period of six calendar months 
preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually 
worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) ninety-five days, in the case of a workman employed below ground in a mine; 
and 
(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case. 


The Photocopy documents filed and proved by the Workman relate to his engagement are only up to the 
period of 204, there is no document filed or proved by the Applicant Workman which indicates that he continued to 
Work till 23.03.206 as alleged by him. Hence, only his statement on oath in support of his this allegation will not be 
sufficient because the Management has also rebutted these allegations in the statement on oath of its witness. Hence, 
in the light of above discussion, the Workman is held to have failed in proving his continuous appointment for 240 
days, in the year preceding the date of his disengagement. 


In the light of above findings, the disengagement of the Workman cannot be held to be unjust or illegal or 
in violation of Section 25F or 25G of the Act. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the petition is liable to be dismissed. 


ORDER 
Petition dismissed. 
No order as to cost.

and from 23..994 to 04.09.2009 and has practiced unfair labour practice in his case by way of violating the 
provisions of Desai Award of 966, Minimum Wages Act, 948, Payment of Wages Act, 938, Bonus Act, 965, and

l. Case R/54/20]] vide notification dated 3.06.20l],

benefits if any he is entitled for?”

Shri Jagdish is just and proper? If yes, what relief the Workman is entitled to?” 


It is further the case of the Management that, case No. R/54/20l] which was against termination of 
services of the Workman Jagdish Chauhan raised on similar grounds in the said dispute has been vide Award dated

Both the sides have filed affidavits as their examination-in-chief. They have been cross-examined by their 
opposite party.

for Management. I have gone through the record as well.

The reference itself is the issue for determination. 


There is Award of R/54/20] in which the termination of the Workman was counter dispute. This Tribunal 
recorded a finding that the Workman could not successful prove his continuous engagement with the Bank for 240 
days in any year, hence his services were not terminated in violation of the Act. 


The Case regarding payment of Bonus is subject matter of different case which is R/l00/202. 
Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code is being reproduced as follows: 


Il. Res judicata.—No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in 
issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties 
under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent 
suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such 
Court. 


Explanation I.—The expression “former suit” shall denote a suit which has been decided prior to a suit in 
question whether or not it was instituted prior thereto. 


Explanation II.—For the purposes of this section, the competence of a Court shall be determined irrespective of 
any provisions as to a right of appeal from the decision of such Court. 


Explanation IlI.—The matter above referred to must in the former suit have been alleged by one party and either 
denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other. 


Explanation IV.—Any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in such 
former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. 


Explanation V.—Any relief claimed in the plaint, which is not expressly granted by the decree, shall for the 
purposes of this section, be deemed to have been refused. 


Explanation VI.—Where persons litigate bona fide in respect of a public right or of a private right claimed in 
common for themselves and others, all persons interested in such right shall, for the purposes of this section, be 
deemed to claim under the persons so litigating . 


Explanation VII.—The provisions of this section shall apply to a proceeding for the execution of a decree and 
references in this section to any suit, issue or former suit shall be construed as references, respectively, to a 
proceeding for the execution of the decree, question arising in such proceeding and a former proceeding for the 
execution of that decree. 


Explanation VIII. —An issue heard and finally decided by a Court of limited jurisdiction, competent to decide 
such issue, shall operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit, notwithstanding that such Court of limited 
jurisdiction was not competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently 
raised. 


Since, the disputes like non-issuing of appointment/termination letter or non preparation of Muster Roll, 
were ancillary, issue connected with the dispute of termination which ought to have been raised in the previous case 
mentioned above. The Workman Union cannot be permitted to raise because it is barred by constructive res judicata. 
The payment of minimum wages is not supported by any evidence from the side of Workman Union, hence, this 
allegation is also held not proved. 


In the light of above discussion and findings, the reference stands answered accordingly. 
No order as to cost.

2. The record of enquiry proceeding goes to reveal that there is ample evidence on record to prove the charges

Tribunal to interfere in the order of the Disciplinary Authority, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of State Bank of 
Bikaner and Jaipur versus Nemi Chand Nalwaya, in Civil Appeal No. 586 of 2007, 20il (4) SCC 584 
decided on March I, 20i, Hon’ble Apex Court have held:- 


“6. It is now well settled that the courts will not act as an appellate court and reassess the evidence led in the 
domestic enquiry, nor interfere on the ground that another view is possible on the material on record. If the 
enquiry has been fairly and properly held and the findings are based on evidence, the question of adequacy of 
the evidence or the reliable nature of the evidence will not be grounds for interfering with the findings in 
departmental enquiries. Therefore, courts will not interfere with findings of fact recorded in departmental 
enquiries, except where such findings are based on no evidence or where they are clearly perverse. The test to 
find out perversity is to see whether a tribunal acting reasonably could have arrived at such conclusion or 
finding, on the material on record. Courts will however interfere with the findings in disciplinary matters, if 
principles of natural justice or statutory regulations have been violated or if the order is found to be arbitrary, 
capricious, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations.” 
In view of law laid down by Hon'ble Apex Court it safely be concluded that finding recorded by Enquiry Officer 
holding charges of misappropriation of loan amount is on the basis of evidence and admission of Petitioner on record. 
Thus, the punishment order does not suffer from any illegality, impropriety or perversity hence, liable to be 
confirmed. 


3. Moreover, as regard seriousness and gravity of charges levelled and proved against Petitioner it cannot be 
said that the charges of misappropriation of funds by the Petitioner is simple in nature. In other words, it is serious

discussed hereunder:- 


Further, in the case of Disciplinary Authority vs. Nikunj Bihari Patnaik JT 996 (4) page 457 Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held:- 


“In the case of a Bank - for that matter, in the case of any other organization - every officer/employee is 
supposed to act within the limits of his authority. If each officer/ employee is allowed to act beyond his 
authority, the discipline of the organisation/bank will disappear; the functioning of the Bank would become 
chaotic and unmanageable. Each officer of the Bank cannot be allowed to carve out his own little empire 
wherein he dispenses favours and largesse. No organization, more particularly, a Bank can function properly 
and effectively if its officers and employees do not observe the prescribed norms and discipline. Such 
indiscipline cannot be condoned on the specious ground that it was not actuated by ulterior motives or by 
extraneous considerations. The very act of acting beyond authority - that too a course of conduct spread over 
a sufficiently long period and involving innumerable instances - is by itself a misconduct. Such acts, if 
permitted, may bring in profit in some cases but they may also lead to huge losses. Such adventures are not 
given to the employees of Banks which deal with public funds. If what we hear about the reasons for the 
collapse of Barings Bank is true, it is attributable to the acts of one of its employees, Nick Leeson, a minor 
officer stationed at Singapore, who was allowed by his superiors to act far beyond his authority. As mentioned 
hereinbefore, the very discipline of an organization and more particularly, a Bank is dependent upon each of 
its employees and officers acting and operating within their allotted sphere. Acting beyond one's authority is 
by itself a breach of discipline and a breach of Regulation 3. It constitutes misconduct within the meaning of 
Regulation 24. No further proof of loss is really necessary though as a matter of fact, in this case there are 
findings that several advances and over-drawals allowed by the Respondent beyond his authority have become 
sticky and irrecoverable. Just because, similar acts have fetched some profit - huge profit, as the High Court 
characterizes it - they are no less blameworthy. It is wrong to characterize them as errors of judgment. It is 
not suggested that the Respondent being a Class-I officer was not aware of the limits of his authority or of his 
powers. Indeed, Charge No.9, which has been held established in full is to the effect that inspite of instructions 
by the Regional Office to stop such practice, the Respondent continued to indulge in such acts. The Enquiry 
Officer has recorded a clear finding that the Respondent did flout the said instructions and has thereby 
committed an act of disobedience of lawful orders. Similarly, Charge No.8, which has also been established in 
full is to the effect that inspite of reminders, the Respondent did not submit "Control Returns" 


to the Regional Office. We fail to understand how could all this be characterized as errors of judgment and not 
as misconduct as defined by the regulations. We are of the opinion that the High Court has committed a clear 
error in holding that the aforesaid conduct of the Respondent does not amount to misconduct or that it does 
not constitute violation of Regulations 3 and 24.”

“Bank officer is required to exercise higher standards of honesty and integrity -Defence that there was no loss of

“ the facts of the case are that the Appellant was working as cashier in the Meerut State branch of State Bank

Appellant workman and authorizing to withdraw the amount Rs.500/-from his account. The said authority 
letter was for withdrawal of Rs.500/-, but, workman acting as cashier manipulated figure in the letter from 
Rs.500/- to 77. /300/- and withdrawn the amount retained 75, /099/- with him. 


In that case enquiry was held and the casual Appellant was dismissed from the job. In the case the alleged 
misconduct of the Appellant to produce forged documents and withdrew 75./300/- instead Rs.500/- and 
Rs.l000/- in excess of the amount which he was not authorized misappropriated it. In that case Appellant 
had submitted his confession letter and on the basis of the confession letter and substantial evidence he was 
terminated from the service and the Hon’ble Apex Court upheld the termination of the Appellant.” Therefore, 
plea of Petitioner that his letter of admission of guilt is not admissible evidence is not tenable.” 


In the case of Darshan Singh Vs. Canara Bank CWP .४०.।०0458/ 2003 D.O.D. 6.4.207 High Court held: 


“the Court has rightly observed that oral evidence contrary to documentary evidence and entries has not to be 
believed this was the case defendant for proof of misconduct on documentary evidence and entries in the Saving 
Bank Account pass book and ledger folios etc... The workman admitted that these entries made by him saying 
that it was made under bonafide mistake. Such act have serious propensities which when made public a bank 
might loss its reputation and confidence in investing public, not continue employment. It was the case of 
misappropriation. Even if it is classified as temporary misappropriation or temporary embezzlement both are

mistake. In the opinion of Labour Court no lenience can be shown to the workman. Once the misconduct is

except in cases where the punishment is so harsh as to suggest victimization.”

# 7, The second reason assigned by the Tribunal that the Enquiry Officer should have allowed the Respondent 
the opportunity to lead evidence in rebuttal is also without substance in the overall facts of the case. The 
Respondent had already tendered two admissions of guilt in writing and one orally before 79.7 and there was

#7, In our considered view, looking into seriousness of the nature of allegations levelled against the 
Respondent employee, the punishment of dismissal inflicted upon him in no manner could be said to be 
shockingly disproportionate which would have required to be interfered with by the Tribunal in exercise of its 
power under Section IIA of the Act 7947. At the same time, merely because the employee stood superannuated 
in the meanwhile, will not absolve him from the misconduct which he had committed in discharge of his duties 
and looking into the nature of misconduct which he had committed, he was not entitled for any indulgence. The 
Bank employee always holds the position of trust where honesty and integrity are the sine qua non but it would 
never be advisable to deal with such matters leniently. 


2, Consequently, the appeal succeeds and is allowed. The interference made by the Tribunal and the High 
Court in the impugned judgment is hereby set aside. No costs.” 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court even a temporary misappropriation of fund of bank by 
the employee amounts to serious and grave misconduct and once proved such charges against employee deserve the 
termination of employment. Further, charges can be held proved on the basis of admission made by CSE. In this 
case, Petitioner has already admitted second charge, hence there is no need for further to discuss here. 


5. Thus, in view of the fore gone discussion and law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court as discussed above, 
both the charges misappropriation and pilfering the official documents of bank being serious in nature therefore, the 
order of punishment of compulsory retirement of the Petitioner passed by Respondent Disciplinary Authority cannot 
be faulted with neither it can be said to be in anyway disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. _ Disciplinary 
Authority has already taken a lenient view in awarding the punishment of compulsory retirement with benefits of 
superannuation. Therefore, the imposition of said punishment cannot be termed as disproportionate to the gravity of 
charges and deserve to be upheld. Thus, the punishment order passed by Disciplinary Authority deserves to be 
upheld and claim petition filed by the Petitioner is devoid of merit he is liable to be dismissed. 


This point is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of the Respondent management.

Section 2577 in The Industrial Disputes Act, 7947 


25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen.- No workman employed in any industry who has been 
in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until— 


(a) the workman has been given one month' s notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the

notice:

days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six months; 
and

specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 


l]. Further, the burden of proof lies on the Petitioner to prove the fact that she has been terminated by the 
Respondent in contravention of provision contained under section 25 F of I.D. Act, 947. In this context, the 
following decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court are relevant as hereunder:- 


In the case of Manager, R.B.I., Bangalore Vs. S. Mani & others AIR 2005 SC 279 the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held:- 


“BURDEN OF PROOF: 


The initial burden of proof was on the workmen to show that they had completed 240 days of service. 


In Range Forest Officer Vs. S.T. Hadimani [(2002) 3 SCC 25], it was stated: 


"3In our opinion the Tribunal was not right in placing the onus on the management without first determining on 
the basis of cogent evidence that the Respondent had worked for more than 240 days in the year preceding his 
termination. It was the case of the claimant that he had so worked but this claim was denied by the appellant. It 
was then for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in the year preceding 
his termination. Filing of an affidavit is only his own statement in his favour and that cannot be regarded as 
sufficient evidence for any court or tribunal to come to the conclusion that a workman had, in fact, worked for 
240 days in a year. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record of appointment or 
engagement for this period was produced by the workman. On this ground alone, the award is liable to be set 
aside. 


[See also Essen Deinki Vs. Rajiv Kumar, (2002) 8 SCC 400] In Siri Niwas (supra), this Court held: 


"The provisions of the Indian Evidence Act per se are not applicable in an industrial adjudication. The general 
principles of it are, however applicable. It is also imperative for the Industrial Tribunal to see that the 
principles of natural justice are complied with. The burden of proof was on the Respondent herein to show that 
he had worked for 240 days in preceding twelve months prior to his alleged retrenchment. In terms of Section 
25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, /947, an order retrenching a workman would not be effective unless the 
conditions precedent therefor are satisfied. Section 25-F postulates the following conditions to be fulfilled by 
employer for effecting a valid retrenchment : 


(i) one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment or wages in lieu thereof; 


(ii) payment of compensation equivalent to fifteen days, average pay for every completed year of continuous 
service or any part thereof in excess of six months." 


Further, in Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court 
held: - 


“It was the case of the workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim 
was denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days 
in the year preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his 
favor and that cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion 
that in fact the claimant had worked for 240 days in a year.” 


In the case of Mohan Lal v. Management, BEL 98 SCC P. 225, Hon'ble Apex Court held, " 


Before a workman can claim retrenchment, not being in consonance of Section 25 of the ID act. he has to show 
that he has been in continuous service of not less than I year with the employer who had retrenched him from 
service." 


580 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


The Hon'ble Apex Court in this case also laid down the principle of how to count 240 days of service 
within one year and held: 


"Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous service for a period of one year despite 
the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered service 
period of 240 days during the period of 72 calendar months for counting backwards and just preceding the 
relevant date being the date of retrenchment. In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause 
(2)(a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant date, ie the date of termination of service which is 
complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained. move backward to a period of 72 months just 
preceding the date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the period of /2 months, the workman 
has rendered service for a period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively answered in favor of the 
workman pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed that the workman 
is in continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in 
Section 25-F". 


In the case of GM., BSNL and others V. Mahesh Chand AIR 2008 SC (Supp) 328, wherein the Hon’ble Apex 
Court have held, 


“Tt was the case of the claimant that he had so worked but this claim was denied by the appellant. It was then for the 
claimant to lead evidence to show that he had in fact worked for 240 days in the year preceding his termination. 
Filing of an affidavit is only his own statement in his favour and that cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for 
any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that a workman had, in fact, worked for 240 days in a year. No proof 
of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record of appointment or engagement for this period was 
produced by the workman. On this ground alone, the award is liable to be set aside.” 


Thus, in view of law laid down by Hon'ble Apex Court as discussed above the initial burden lies upon the Petitioner 
Workman to prove that she had worked for 240 days continuously in a year just preceding the date of her termination. 
But Petitioner has not produced any documentary evidence i.e., any appointment letter issued by Respondent १०.। or 
any salary slip or wage payment slip or attendance register to establish the fact that she had worked in the branch of 
Respondent bank for the alleged period. Mere filing of the chief statement affidavit of witness is not sufficient to 
corroborate the claim of the Petitioner as she has alleged in the petition. 


2. It is settled the law that the documentary evidence of appointment letter or salary slip or attendance register 
are required to prove the fact of 240 days in continuous service of the Respondent employment just preceding from 
the date of termination. Therefore, for the want of aforementioned documentary evidence, the claim of the Petitioner 
that she was under the employment of Respondent ४०. continuously and had worked for 9 years in the Bank of the 
Respondent, is not proved and established. Therefore, the claim of the Petitioner that she has been terminated in 
contravention of the provision contained under section 25 F is not acceptable as she failed to prove the condition 
precedent as provided under section 25 F for alleged retrenchment. Moreover, MW] states that Petitioner was never 
appointed by the Respondent No.! as such there is no question of termination of her services by the bank by one 
month’s notice nor any retrenchment compensation as she was never appointed by the bank, hence, there arises no 
question of termination of her services by the bank. Therefore, in view of the fore gone discussion and law laid 
down by the Hon'ble Apex Court as discussed above, this issue is decided against the Workman Petitioner.

2. 


As regards the plea of the Workman that there is no sufficient evidence on record, in this context it is settled 


law that question of adequacy of evidence or reliable nature of evidence will not be agreed for interfering with the 
finding in the Departmental Enquiry unless such findings are based on no evidence or where they are clearly 
perverse. 


In State of Bikaner & Jaipur Vs. Nemi Chand Nalwaya in Civil Appeal No.586/2007 AIR 20 SC 93 dated 
.3.200I is relevant wherein the Hon’ble Apex Court have held:- 


“6. It is now well settled that the courts will not act as an appellate court and reassess the evidence led in the 
domestic Enquiry, nor interfere on the ground that another view is possible on the material on record. If the 
Enquiry has been fairly and properly held and the findings are based on evidence, the question of adequacy of 
the evidence or the reliable nature of the evidence will not be grounds for interfering with the findings in 
departmental enquiries. Therefore, courts will not interfere with findings of fact recorded in departmental 
enquiries, except where such findings are based on no evidence or where they are clearly perverse. The test to 
find out perversity is to see whether a tribunal acting reasonably could have arrived at such conclusion or 
finding, on the material on record. Courts will however interfere with the findings in disciplinary matters, if 
principles of natural justice or statutory regulations have been violated or if the order is found to be arbitrary, 
capricious, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations.” 


Further, in the case of State of Rajasthan Vs. Heem Singh, Civil Appeal No.3340/2020, (supra) Hon’ble Apex 
Court have held:- 


33. In exercising judicial review in disciplinary matters, there are two ends of the spectrum. The first embodies 
a rule of restraint. The second defines when interference is permissible. The rule of restraint constricts the 
ambit of judicial review. This is for a valid reason. The determination of whether a misconduct has been 
committed lies primarily within the domain of the disciplinary authority. The judge does not assume the mantle 
of the disciplinary authority. Nor does the judge wear the hat of an employer. Deference to a finding of fact by 
the disciplinary authority is a recognition of the idea that it is the employer who is responsible for the efficient 
conduct of their service. Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not 
governed by strict rules of evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the 
strict standard which governs a criminal trial, of proof beyond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed 
by a preponderance of probabilities. Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on 
context and subject... ... ... ..... That is to satisfy the conscience of the court that there is some evidence to support 
the charge of misconduct and to guard against perversity. But this does not allow the court to re-appreciate 
evidentiary findings in a disciplinary Enquiry or to substitute a view which appears to the judge to be more 
appropriate. To do so would offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the 
exercise of robust common sense without which the judges’ craft is in vain.” 


In the case of State of Haryana versus Rattan Singh 977 ACC page 49 while dealing with the standard of proof/ 
Evidence applicable in domestic enquiry Hon'ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“4. It is well settled that in a domestic enquiry the strict and sophisticated rules of evidence under the Indian 
Evidence Act may not apply. Ail materials which are logically probative for a prudent mind are permissible. 
There is no allergy to hearsay evidence provided it has reasonable nexus and credibility. It is true that 
departmental authorities and administrative tribunals must be careful in evaluating such material and should 
not glibly swallow what is strictly speaking not relevant under the Indian Evidence Act. For this proposition it 
is not necessary to cite decisions nor text books, although we have been taken through case law and other 
authorities by counsel on both sides. The essence of a judicial approach is objectivity, exclusion of extraneous 
materials or considerations and observance of rules of natural justice. Of course, fairplay is the basis and if 
perversity or arbitrariness, bias or surrender of independence of judgment vitiate the conclusions reached, such 
finding,even though of a domestic tribunal, cannot be held good. However, the courts below mis-directed 
themselves, perhaps, in insisting that passengers who had come in and gone out should be chased and brought 
before the tribunal before a valid finding could be recorded. The 'residuum' rule to which counsel for the 


[भाग व--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाह़ 2, 947 59] 


respondent referred, based upon certain passengers from American jurisprudence does not go to that extent nor 
does the passage from Halsbury insist on such rigid requirement. The simple point is, was there some evidence 
or was there no evidence not in the sense of the technical rules governing regular court proceedings but in a 
fair common-sense way as men of understanding and wordly wisdom will accept. Viewed in this way, 
sufficiency of evidence in proof of the finding by a domestic tribunal is beyond scrutiny. Absence of any 
evidence in support of a ending is certainty available for the court to look into because it amounts to an error of 
law apparent on the record. We find, in this case, that the evidence of Chamanlal, Inspector of the flying squad, 
is some evidence which has elevance to the charge leveled against the respondent. Therefore, we are unable to 
hold that the order is invalid on that ground. “ 


Thus, in view of the principle laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above the Tribunal has got no 
jurisdiction to reassess the evidence lead in the domestic enquiry nor to interfere on the ground that another view is 
possible on the material on record. In the present case enquiry has been fairly and properly held and findings are 
based on evidence. It is not the case that the finding of the Enquiry Officer is based on no evidence or suffers from 
perversity. Therefore, there is no ground in the present matter to interfere in the finding recorded by the Enquiry 
Officer and also to set aside punishment order passed by Disciplinary Authority on the basis of that finding. 


3. Further, as regards the plea of the Petitioner that the imposition of punishment is disproportionate to the 
charge levelled against the Petitioner, in this context Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Om Kumar vs. Union 
Of India 200 (SCC) 2 386 have held:- 


“The question of quantum of punishment in disciplinary matters is primarily for the disciplinary authority to 
order and the jurisdiction of the High courts under Article 226 of the Constitution or of the Administrative 
Tribunals is limited and is confined to the applicability of one or other of the well known principles known as 
“Wednesbury principles”. Further, it is held in the Wednesbury case, ((9486)7 KB 223 it was said when a 
statute gave discretion to an administrator to take a decision, the scope of judicial review would remain limited. 
Lord Greene further said that interference was not permissible unless one or the other of the following 
conditions was satisfied namely, 7) the order was contrary law, or 2) relevant factors were not considered, or 
3) irrelevant factors were considered, or 4) the decision was one which no reasonable person could have 
taken.” 


Further in the case of BC Chaturvedi vs. Union of India 995(6) SCC 749 in paragraph |8 Supreme Court have 
held:- 


776, A review of the above legal position would establish that the disciplinary authority, and on appeal the 
appellate authority, being fact-finding authorities have exclusive power to consider the evidence with a view to 
maintain discipline. They are invested with the discretion to impose appropriate punishment keeping in view the 
magnitude or gravity of the misconduct. The High Court/Tribunal, while exercising the power of judicial 
review, cannot normally substitute its own conclusion on penalty and impose some other penalty. If the 
punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority or the appellate authority shocks the conscience of the High 
Court/Tribunal, it would appropriately mould the relief, either directing the disciplinary/appellate authority to 
reconsider the penalty imposed, or to shorten the litigation, it may itself, in exceptional and rare cases, impose 
appropriate punishment with cogent reasons in support thereof." 


Further, in the case of General Secretary, South Indian Cashew Factory Workers Union vs Kerala State 
Cashew Development, 2006 LLR page 657 Hon’ble Supreme Court have held that if the enquiry is fair and proper 
and in the absence of any allegation of victimization, the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to interfere in the order of 
punishment. 


Further, reference of the case of the United Bank of India vs. Bachan Prasad Lal Civil Appeal No. 2949 of 20 
date of decision .2.2022, is relevant in this context. The facts of the case are that workman CSE was the bank 
employee and he fraudulently prepared 9 credit transfer vouchers on various dates on the pretext of payment of 
interest towards fixed deposits and crediting the whole amount to one saving account opened in the name of one 
Smt.Asha Devi (admittedly the fake account prepared by Respondent employee). In order to adjust the said amount 
he manipulated the other book records of the bank using forged signatures. After such nature of allegations stood 
proved, the disciplinary authority after taking into consideration the record of inquiry and the post held by the 
Respondent employee, imposed the punishment to employee with the penalty of dismissal from service. In that case 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


ढ#॥7, In our considered view, looking into seriousness of the nature of allegations levelled against the 
Respondent employee, the punishment of dismissal inflicted upon him in no manner could be said to be 
shockingly disproportionate which would have required to be interfered with by the Tribunal in exercise of its 
power under Section //4 of the Act 7947, At the same time, merely because the employee stood superannuated 
in the meanwhile, will not absolve him from the misconduct which he had committed in discharge of his duties 
and looking into the nature of misconduct which he had committed, he was not entitled for any indulgence. The 
Bank employee always holds the position of trust where honesty and integrity are the sine qua non but it would 


592 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY 2, 2025/ASHADHA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


never be advisable to deal with such matters leniently. 


2, Consequently, the appeal succeeds and is allowed. The interference made by the Tribunal and the High 
Court in the impugned judgment is hereby set aside. No costs.” 


Further, the reference of the SBI vs Hemant Kumar 20]! (4) SCC 355, is relevant therein workmen worked in the 
appellant bank as cashier cum clerk and it was discovered that the Respondent had been indulging in misappropriation 
of money by making fictitious entries and manipulations in the bank’s ledgers. The departmental enquiry was 
conducted against the Workman and Enquiry Officer submitted his report holding the Respondent guilty of all the 
charges. The appeal was also dismissed. CSE workman preferred appeal against the order of Disciplinary Authority 
and during the pendency of the appeal CSE workman submitted a letter admitting his guilt in writing, presumably 
hoping that a lenient view would be taken in the appeal but the appeal was also dismissed. The matter was referred 
for adjudication to the Tribunal and Tribunal set aside the dismissal order of the bank employee and ordered for 
reinstatement with full back wages. In that case Supreme Court have held:- 


#॥॥, The second reason assigned by the Tribunal that the Enquiry Officer should have allowed the Respondent the 
opportunity to lead evidence in rebuttal is also without substance in the overall facts of the case. The Respondent had 
already tendered two admissions of guilt in writing and one orally before 77.7 and there was hardly anything that 
could be said on his behalf to repel the charges. 


42. We are, therefore, satisfied that the Tribunal's findings are wholly unreasonable and perverse and fit to be set 
aside. The High Court, unfortunately, did not consider the matter as it should have, in light of the discussions made 
above. The High Court's order is equally unsustainable. We, accordingly, set aside the order passed by the High 
Court and the award made by the Tribunal. The appeal is allowed but with no order as to costs.”’ 


4. At this juncture it would be pertinent to mention the para 5(j) of the bipartite settlement dated 0.4.2002 
which provides, 


“5. By the expression” gross misconduct” shall be meant any of the following acts and omissions and the part of 
an employee: 


Para(j):- doing any act prejudicial to the interest of the bank or gross negligence or negligence involving or likely 
to involve the bank in serious loss;” 


Para 6 of the bipartite settlement provides, 
“6, An employee found guilty of gross misconduct may: 
(a) be dismissed without notice; or 


(9) be removed from service with superannuation benefits i.e., pension and/or Provident fund and gratuity as 
would be due otherwise under the rules or regulations prevailing at the relevant time and without disqualification 
from future employment; or 


(c) be compulsorily retired with superannuation benefits i.e., pension and/or Provident fund and gratuity as would 
be due otherwise under the rules or regulations prevailing at the relevant time and without disqualification from 
future employment; or” 


Thus, the Petitioner Workman has been found guilty of committing misconduct and has been awarded the 
punishment as per the bipartite settlement para 6(c) and there is no illegality or infirmity and perversity in the 
impugned order of punishment. 


5. Moreover, the record of enquiry goes to reveal that the Petitioner has submitted his written reply dated nil in 
response to the chargesheet dated 5.8.2009 and in his reply he has admitted that he has made some entries by mistake 
in usual and routine manner by using his ID and all entries were authorised by Manager, he had neither used the user 
ID of the Manager nor authorised the entries as alleged. Further, he stated that as the balance was available in his 
account he has availed the amount and when it came to his notice that there was a wrong credit in his account he had 
adjusted the amount. Further, he stated that he had not done any fraudulent transaction and there is no loss either to 
the bank or to anybody as the amount was appropriated. Thus, in his reply to the chargesheet he has admitted that on 
25.0.2008 at a given time in the charge sheet he has created and entered the transaction unauthorisedly using ID of 
the Manager as detailed in the charge sheet. Thus, in view of the documentary and oral evidence on record and also 
admission of the Petitioner Workman, it is established that workman has committed gross misconduct as described in 
Para 5(j) of Bipartite Settlement and there is no illegality or infirmity in the punishment order passed by the 
Respondent bank. 


6. Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court as discussed above, in the present matter there 
is ample evidence on record apart from admission made by CSE in support of the charge against the Petitioner and 
disciplinary authority has rightly imposed the punishment of “compulsorily retired with superannuation benefits i.e., 
pension and /or provident fund and gratuity as would be due otherwise under the rules are regulations prevailing at 
the relevant time and without disqualifications from future employment” by taking lenient view. In the facts and 
circumstances of the case in my considered opinion the punishment imposed upon workman is not disproportionate 
and rather commensurate to the gravity of charges levelled against CSE workman. 


[भाग II—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई 2, 2025/आषाढ़ 2, 947 593 


This issue is decided accordingly against the Petitioner workman and in favour of the Respondent. 


7. Issue No.III:- In view of the fore gone discussion and finding arrived at Issue No.II, the Petitioner has 
been found guilty of committing misconduct under Para 5(j) of Bipartite Settlement and has rightly been punished 
with order of “compulsorily retired with superannuation benefits i.e., pension and /or provident fund and gratuity as 
would be due otherwise under the rules are regulations prevailing at the relevant time and without disqualifications 
from future employment”. Therefore, he is not entitled for any relief and his petition is liable to be dismissed. 


This issue is answered accordingly. 


AWARD 


In view of the fore gone discussion and finding arrived at Issue Nos.I & IH, I am of the considered view 
that the action of the Respondent in imposing the punishment of “compulsorily retired with superannuation benefits 
i.e., pension and /or provident fund and gratuity as would be due otherwise under the rules are regulations prevailing 
at the relevant time and without disqualifications from future employment” to the Petitioner Sri PJC. Bhanudev is 
legal and justified. Hence, the Petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. As such, the petition filed by the 
Petitioner deserves to be dismissed as devoid of merits. Therefore, the petition is dismissed. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

सं. 9-73/2025-4.3(0)—srath, केन्द्र सरकार को विश्वविद्यालय अनुदान आयोग (यूजीसी) अधिनियम, 4956 की धारा 3 के तहत 
विश्वविद्यालय अनुदान आयोग की सलाह पर उच्चतर शिक्षण संस्था को सम विश्वविद्यालय संस्था के रूप में घोषित करने की शक्ति प्राप्त है। 


2. और जबकि, यूजीसी अधिनियम, 7956 की धारा 3 के तहत क्रिस्टु जयंती, के. नारायणपुरा, कोठानूर पीओ, बेंगलुरु, कर्नाटक के 
नाम पर सामान्य श्रेणी के तहत सम विश्वविद्यालय संस्था का दर्जा देने के लिए यूजीसी के पोर्टल पर बोधि निकेतन ट्रस्ट द्वारा दिनांक 34.70.2023 
को एक ऑनलाइन आवेदन प्रस्तुत किया गया। 


3. और जबकि, यूजीसी ने दिनांक 77.04.2025 के अपने पत्र संख्या 26-5/2023 (सीपीपी-॥/डीयू) के माध्यम से सूचित किया कि 
यूजीसी (सम विश्वविद्यालय संस्था) विनियम, 2023 के अनुसार इसकी विशेषज्ञ समिति द्वारा आवेदन की जांच की गई। विशेषज्ञ समिति ने पाया 
कि क्रिस्टु जयंती, बेंगलुरु, कर्नाटक के एनएएसी प्रत्यायन के दूसरे और तीसरे चक्र में अंतर है, इसलिए, समिति ने यूजीसी विनियम, 2023 के 
तहत सम विश्वविद्यालय संस्था का दर्जा देने की सिफारिश नहीं की। 


4. और आगे जबकि, मंत्रालय ने दिनांक 03.06.2025 के पत्र के माध्यम से संस्था द्वारा पात्रता शर्तों को पूरा करने के संबंध में यूजीसी 
से कुछ स्पष्टीकरण का अनुरोध किया। उत्तर में, यूजीसी ने दिनांक 23.06.2025 के अपने पत्र संख्या 26-5/2023 (सीपीपी-॥/डीयू) के माध्यम से

No. 9-3/2025-U.3(A)—Whereas, the Central Government is empowered under Section 3 of the University Grants 
Commission (UGC) Act, |956 to declare, on the advice of the UGC, an Institution of higher learning as an Institution deemed 
to be University. 


2. And whereas, an online application dated 3.0.2023 was submitted by Bodhi Niketan Trust on UGC’s Portal for 
grant of Institution Deemed to be University status under general Category in the name of Kristu Jayanti, K. Narayanapura, 
Kothanur P O, Bengaluru, Karnataka under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 956. 


3. And whereas, UGC, vide its letter No. 26-5/2023 (CPP-I/DU) dated .04.2025, informed that the application was 
examined by its Expert committee in accordance with the UGC (Institutions deemed to be Universities) Regulations, 2023. The 
Expert Committee observed that there is a gap of 2nd and 3rd cycle of NAAC Accreditation of Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru, 
Karnataka, hence, the Committee did not recommend for deemed to be University status under the UGC Regulations, 2023. 


4. And further whereas, Ministry, vide letter dated 03.06.2025 requested certain clarification from UGC regarding 
fulfilment of eligibility conditions by the Institution. In response, UGC vide its letter No. 26-5/2023(CPP-I/DU) 
dated 23.06.2025 informed that the gap period between two cycles of NAAC accreditation was condoned by NAAC in case of 
Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru, Karnataka. 


5. Now, therefore, in exercise of powers conferred under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 956, the Ministry of Education, 
considering the clarifications provided by UGC, hereby declares Kristu Jayanti, K. Narayanapura, Kothanur P O, Bengaluru, 
Karnataka as an Institution deemed to be University under general category. The said declaration is subject to the following 
conditions: 


L. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall not admit students in the professional courses before obtaining the approval of 
relevant statutory body, wherever applicable. 


ii. There shall be no diversion of assets or funds/revenues of the Institution deemed to be University/or of its 
constituent teaching units, without prior permission of the UGC and Ministry of Education. 


iii. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall not engage or indulge in any activities that are of commercial and profit making 
in nature. 


iv. The academic programmes to be offered at Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall conform to the norms and standards 
prescribed by the UGC and the Statutory Councils/Bodies concerned. 


v.  Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall align its courses with National Education Policy-2020. 


vi. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall take all the required steps to get all the eligible academic courses/programmes 
rated for valid accreditation by National Board of Accreditation (NBA) and the Institute to get valid accreditation 
by National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC), as the case may be, in terms of the provisions as 
contained in the UGC (Institutions Deemed to be Universities) Regulations, 2023, as amended from time to 
time. 


vii. All the prescribed norms and procedures of the Statutory Councils concerned in the matter of admission of 
students, intake capacity of students, renewal of approval to the academic course / programme, revision of intake 
capacity of students, starting of new courses / programmes, etc. shall continue to be in force, and shall be adhered 
to by Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru. 

viii. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall submit MoA in accordance with UGC (Institutions Deemed to be Universities) 
Regulations, 2023 to UGC. Further, as and when necessary, it shall update or revise or modify its MoA / Rules, 
as per the provisions of the prevailing Regulations. 

ix. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall follow the fee structure as per the Rules and Regulations of the UGC and relevant 
Statutory Councils. 

x.  Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall participate in annual Indian rankings issued by National Institutional Ranking 
Framework (NIRF) of this Ministry. 

xl. Kristu Jayanti, Bengaluru shall compulsorily create Academic Bank of Credits (ABC), identities of their students 
and upload their credit score in digital lockers and ensure that the credit scores are reflected in ABC Portal and 
adopt Samarth e-Gov.
